title: Hours of Idleness
alternative_titles: Hours of Idleness; Original and Translated
description: The first book of verse by a noble minor, gathered from school exercises, imitations and occasional poems written between the Harrow years and the coming of age. It mixes lyric meditations, verse epistles to friends and relations, elegies on the dead, descriptive pieces on Newstead Abbey and translations from the classics and from French. The prevailing manner is that of the sentimental school of the 1790s: a sensitive young poet, estranged from his schoolfellows, consoling himself with memory, friendship and the pleasure of verse. Its hostile review in 1808, and the satirical reply it provoked, turned a private printed book into the opening quarrel of the poet's public career.
plot_or_argument: The volume has no sustained argument but is arranged as a miscellany, opening with odes and lyric meditations and passing through epistles, elegies on friends and dead kinsfolk, and descriptive verse on the abbey and the Harrow playing-field. Its recurring subjects are the loss of schoolfellows, the isolation of a boy among boys, the deaths of maternal relatives in Scotland, and a claim to feeling refined by misfortune. Several pieces address the poet's half-sister directly, and a group of epistles is written to Harrow friends, among them a schoolmate who became a lifelong companion. The close turns on the poet's own prospects and on the consolation of verse, in a diction borrowed from the Scottish school of Beattie and from Campbell. The imitation of prior poets, ancient and modern, is not concealed but presented as the honest exercise of an undeclared hand.
narrative_structure: A miscellany in three loose groups, odes and lyric meditations, then epistles and elegies, then translations and imitations; the ordering is by mood and manner rather than theme, and the 1808 issue added prose argument in the form of a prefatory advertisement.
principal_characters: the poet-speaker; the half-sister addressed in several poems; the Harrow schoolfellows of the epistles; the dead kinswomen of the elegies; the ghost of the abbey in its descriptive piece
literary_form: Juvenile verse miscellany: pre-Romantic sensibility lyric and verse epistle in the manner of the 1790s school of sensibility, with Augustan translation and imitation as its display of education.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly iambic pentameter couplets and quatrains, with irregular ode stanzas, an imitation of the walk-verse of the country poem, and a few lyric measures in the manner of song; the handling is competent and heavily modelled rather than inventive.
historical_context: Printed at a provincial press in 1807 at the author's cost for private circulation, the book was refused by the publisher whom its dedicatee had served, and its augmented London issue of 1808 drew the severe Edinburgh Review notice of April of that year, which treated a noble minor's private verses as public folly. The attack, and the satirical answer it produced, exemplify the new power of the review journals to make or wound a career, and the sensitivity of class, patronage and the booksellers' market in the years of the anti-Jacobin settlement.
literary_significance: It is the documentary starting point of a career that became the most famous in European poetry within five years, and the evidence that the later manner was an argument with the school of sensibility rather than an inheritance from it. Its reviews fixed the posture of the insulted young nobleman that the satire of 1809 exploited and that the pilgrimage poem later dramatized. It also preserves the private mythology of family, home and loss on which the public pose of the tale poems was built.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume appeared over the author's peerage title and initials, and pieces from it were reused and revised in the collected editions.
bibliographical_notes: First printed privately at Newark-on-Trent in 1807 under the title 'Fugitive Pieces', and reissued in the same year with additions as 'Hours of Idleness'; an augmented London edition with a prefatory advertisement, and a price in the bookshops, followed in 1808 and was the edition the reviews attacked. A nineteenth-century variorum of the complete poetical works (1980-93) records the cancellations and revisions.

title: English Bards and Scotch Reviewers
description: A verse satire in heroic couplets, issued anonymously in 1809, which answers the review journals and the living poets of the day in the manner of the Augustan satires of dulness. It moves from a general complaint about the decay of letters to a roll-call of named contemporaries, then to an attack on the critical ascendancy of the northern journals and on the booksellers who pay for reputation. The personal notes of the earlier volume's reception give the whole its motive of insulted honour. It was greatly enlarged in successive issues and then disowned, so that the poet's own collected editions ceased to print it.
plot_or_argument: The satire opens on the degraded state of English letters and passes to a catalogue of the living poets, the lake school and its 'cast-off devotional' followers, the complacency of the laureate, the opium and unfulfilled promises of a distinguished critic-poet, and the merely popular singers, each disposed of in a couplet or two. It then turns on the reviewers of the northern journals, on the booksellers and their patronage, and on the Scottish critical dominance that had judged the first book. A passage of bitter prospect, of exile and of the writer's loneliness, gives way in later issues to an enlarged attack on the neoclassical school of the quietist critics and on the poetasters of the day. The argument is not systematic but cumulative: taste, money and criticism are shown to have corrupted each other, and the satirist claims the right to answer insult in kind.
narrative_structure: A single continuous satire in the epistle manner of the Dunciad and the Art of Criticism, moving from general complaint to enumerated personal attack, with interpolated apostrophes, an argument in verse prefixed to the second issue, and notes added in the enlarged editions.
principal_characters: the satirist-speaker; the personified Muse of England; the avenging figure of Cursery at the close
literary_form: Augustan verse satire and personal catalogue; mock-heroic invective in the restored couplet, with the prosopopoeia and the retreating apostrophe of the didactic poem.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, closed and antithetical, with triplets, alexandrines and a frequent satiric use of the name dropped into the line; the handling is consciously that of the late seventeenth and eighteenth century couplet school.
historical_context: Published in the interval between the reviews of the first volume and the fame of the pilgrimage poem, it belongs to the rowdy Regency book trade in which anonymous personal satire was both a commercial and a legal risk. Its targets were the Edinburgh and Critical journals, the quarterly reviewers, and the lake poets, then at the height of their reputation, and its charge of northern usurpation voiced a real anxiety about metropolitan literary control. Its later suppression, at the point when the author's relations with the trade and with his former opponents were repaired, made the poem a notorious crux of self-censorship.
literary_significance: It showed that a poet of twenty-one could master the closed couplet of the age of Pope, and it installed the satiric personae that the later narrative and romantic irony of the Don Juan period would wear again. Its roll-call is one of the most quoted documents of contemporary reputation, and its history of enlargement and suppression is a case study in the revision of youthful malice by a famous author. It also fixed the quarrel with the northern journals that the pilgrim poem was to convert into a politics of exile.
attribution_notes: Issued anonymously; attribution rests on the author's own later acknowledgement to a friend and on the revision history recorded in the manuscript and letters, and is uncontested in scholarship.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1809 in quarto, anonymously, and reissued the same year with an enlarged text and an epistle in verse, then again in 1810 and 1811 with further additions and notes; a dedication to a school friend was prefixed from the second issue. Withdrawn by its author from the collected editions after 1815 and restored to the canon only by modern variorum editors.

title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Cantos I and II
alternative_titles: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the First and Second
description: The poem that made its author famous overnight: a narrative of travel and refusal in Spenserian stanzas, following an imagined young nobleman through Iberia and the Greek lands while the poet speaks in his own person in the interpolated stanzas and appended epistles. It converts a two-year tour in the Mediterranean into a meditation on national character, on the wreck of the Napoleonic wars, and on the weariness of a sinner who leaves his own country. The hero is at once a portrait of the fashionable outlaw and a mask the poet can step behind, and the mixture of journal, description and confession proved irresistibly quotable.
plot_or_argument: Harold, sated with pleasure, dissipation and some unconfessed guilt, leaves his native country and travels as a spectator and volunteer through the Iberian peninsula, where the poem surveys the sufferings of Portugal and Spain under French invasion and the character of their people. He passes to Greece and the archipelago, where the ruins of Athens, the plain of Troy, the Albanian shore and the living customs of Greek, Slav and Turk supply meditation on liberty, decay and the transience of fame. An affectionate episode and the death of a companion interrupt the journey, and the cantos close with the pilgrim's withdrawal from society and the poet's farewell to the scenes he has described. The governing argument is that the ruined and war-torn south reflects and satisfies a mind already estranged from its own country, and that the poet's own guilt can be displayed only when disguised as another man's.
narrative_structure: Two cantos of traveling meditation, loosely progressive and episodic, with the pilgrim's story told in outline and the lyric effusions, apostrophes and appended epistles carrying the emotional argument; explanatory notes by the poet document the places and translate the passages of foreign speech.
principal_characters: Childe Harold; the poet-speaker who overtakes his own character; the lady of Canto I; the companion who dies on the journey; the Spanish peasant and his daughter; the guides and boatmen of the Greek waters
literary_form: Romantic travel poem and verse romance of exile in the Spenserian stanza, combining the topographical meditation, the domestic tale and the personal effusion; its model of the melancholy, secretive outlaw became a stock of the century.
meter_and_prosody: Nine-line Spenserian stanzas, iambic pentameter with a closing alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc, taken from the romance and meditation tradition and used for sustained description, with a strong caesura, rhetorical apostrophe and an habitual turn of the last line.
historical_context: The cantos were written from the notebooks of a tour made between 1809 and 1811, through Portugal and Spain at the height of the Peninsular war and into Albania and Greece under Ali Pasha, and published in 1812 during the last years of the struggle against Napoleon. The poem's sympathy with Spanish and Greek resistance, and its contempt for the northern journals, addressed a public that had followed the war in the reviews and prints. Its instant fame, quoted in the fashionable and the radical press alike, made the poet's biography a public commodity from the first week of sale.
literary_significance: It created the Byronic hero in narrative form, and fixed the Romantic association of southern landscape, political oppression and imaginative exile; its Spenserian measure was widely imitated in long poems of travel and reflection through the nineteenth century. Its blend of description, note and self-quotation also made it a central exhibit in the contemporary argument between a poetry of sensation and a poetry of description.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the text exists in several authorially revised issues of the 1810s, with cancelled stanzas on the poet's private history suppressed from the first text and restored only by modern editors.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1812 in quarto by the house that remained the poet's publisher for the rest of his life, with the two cantos complete and a prefatory advertisement; many editions followed during the author's lifetime, and the standard scholarly text is the variorum complete poetical works (1980-93).

title: The Giaour
alternative_titles: The Giaour: A Fragment of a Turkish Tale
description: The first and shortest of the oriental tale poems, subtitled 'a Fragment of a Turkish Tale' and set in Greece under Turkish rule. A Christian lover has seduced and abandoned the daughter of a Turkish lord, who drowns her in the sea; the lover lives in a monastery under a curse and in terror of the dead woman's coming judgment, and is finally killed by her father in a mountain encounter. The poem establishes the outlaw, the haunted guilty self and the eastern landscape as a theatre of conscience. Its manner is not narrative continuity but a sequence of vivid fragments, songs and interpolated voices.
plot_or_argument: The story is given in pieces and by shifting narrators: an opening description of the evening sea, the drowned girl's funeral and the mourning songs, the father's quest for revenge, and then the long encounter at the hermit's cell in which the outlaw tells his own history of seduction, desertion and the beloved's death. The Turkish lord slays him, and he dies unreconciled under the monk's curse, while the villagers declare that the vampire of the drowned girl haunts the shore. The argument is less a tale than a study of guilt without repentance, of a will that refuses the church's remedy, and of revenge as the only honour left to an eastern lord. The interpolated songs, on the happiness of the fisherman's life and on the roses and nightingales of the east, offer a lyric counterworld to the tragedy.
narrative_structure: A deliberately fragmentary sequence of set pieces, told now by a fisherman, now by a monk, now by the Giaour himself, with ballad songs and a concluding apostrophe on the superstitious credulity of the Greek villagers.
principal_characters: the Giaour; the Turkish lord, father of the drowned girl; the drowned girl; the hermit of the cell; the fisherman and the Greek villagers
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the oriental or gothic tale poem, with the interpolated popular song and the supernatural credulity of the ballad tradition.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, broken by interpolated songs and lyric stanzas of popular measure, with anapestic variation in the passages of supernatural terror.
historical_context: Written and published within two months of the poet's separation from his wife and the public scandal that followed his departure from England, the tale converted the materials of the recent tour into a drama of unpardonable sin. The Greek cause, the Albanian court of a local pasha and the current taste for eastern scenery supplied both its subject and its market, and its success fixed the couplet-tale as the form of popular poetry for a decade. Its treatment of seduction and its hostile portraits of monastic remedy drew moral criticism from the quarterly press.
literary_significance: It set the pattern of the verse tale, guilty hero, eastern scene and fragmented narration, that the sequel tales and the whole school of popular romance in verse imitated. It also gave the century its first great study of a conscience that refuses forgiveness, and its vampire and superstition passages fed the gothic imagination of the following decades.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was revised and enlarged across several issues in the author's lifetime, and the suppressed lines concerning the heroine's fate are recorded in the variorum.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1813 as a small quarto, printed at the private press used for the earliest tales and sold by the poet's regular house; the text was enlarged and the arrangement altered in the issues of the same year and of 1814.

title: The Bride of Abydos
alternative_titles: The Bride of Abydos: A Turkish Tale
description: The second oriental tale, set at Abydos on the Hellespont and built on a love between a half-brother and half-sister who do not know their kinship. The girl is promised to the old pasha who holds her father's life in pawn, and the lovers attempt a flight by sea that ends in pursuit and death. The poem is the most lyrical of the tales, rich in song, apostrophe to the nightingale and the rose, and in imagery of the water, the moon and the veil. It was written out of the poet's own domestic crisis, and the theme of forbidden affection is handled with an unusual frankness.
plot_or_argument: The young warrior loves the daughter of the same father by another mother, believing her only his sister in name, and the pasha of Abydos demands her in marriage as the price of her father's safety. The lovers plan escape across the straits; the father discovers the kinship and dies of the shock, and the pasha pursues in the night, finding the two locked together on the shore and killing the youth before the girl dies of grief. The argument turns on the guilt of desire that is innocent of knowledge, on the commerce in women that the eastern court practises, and on the faithless protection of fathers. Lyric interruptions, including the songs of the harem and the apostrophe to the hour of love, slow the plot in favour of mood.
narrative_structure: Two short cantos in continuous couplet narrative with embedded songs and dramatic addresses, the exposition compressed and the crisis deferred by lyric reflection.
principal_characters: the youth of Abydos; his half-sister and bride; their father, a lord in the pasha's power; the pasha of Abydos; the slave and confidante of the harem
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the oriental love tale, with the interpolated song and the domestic tragedy of concealed kinship.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter for the narrative, with lyric stanzas of shorter measure for the songs and a marked use of repetition and exclamation in the passages of alarm.
historical_context: Published before the end of 1813 and at once attacked by the quarterly press for its treatment of incest and for its oriental licence, the poem belongs to the moment when the exile's private history had become a matter of public speculation and when the Turkish tale was the most saleable verse form in Britain. The second issue of 1814, greatly enlarged, doubled its length and gave the poem its final shape.
literary_significance: It carried the guilty-hero tale into the region of innocent and unknowing transgression, and its lyrics made it one of the most widely set and quoted of the tales, with songs that entered the popular repertoire. Its frank handling of a forbidden affection became a permanent scandal of the poet's reputation and a test case for the argument about the relation of life and work.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the 1813 first issue and the much enlarged 1814 second issue are both authorial, and the differences are recorded in the variorum.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1813, printed for the author and sold by his regular publisher, in a small quarto; a second edition, with some three hundred additional lines, appeared in 1814.

title: The Corsair
description: The most immediately successful of the verse tales, selling tens of thousands of copies on the day of publication. A pirate chief, famous for a hardness that spares no enemy, discovers that a captive has won his wife's pity, and in a crisis of jealousy commits a private murder on the island of his followers. He then returns to the scene of his youth, is taken by the lord of the island, and perishes in a burning convent whose aisles shelter his bride. The tale turns the outlaw's career into a study of a love that cannot survive knowledge of itself.
plot_or_argument: The pirate is a lord of the archipelago, dreaded and obeyed, whose one tie is to the woman who has softened his ferocity; hearing that she has pitied a prisoner, he steals at night to the cave and kills him. The murdered man's lord pursues him to the isle where he was born, and the pirate is taken and condemned; he escapes by night to the convent where his bride waits, and the building is fired about them, so that they perish together in the aisles while the islanders watch. The argument is that a nature formed for command is destroyed by the one sentiment that makes it human, and that concealment, not guilt, is the outlaw's real condition. The meditations on the sea, the cave and the mind's secret history carry the poem far beyond its plot.
narrative_structure: Three cantos of compact narrative, opened by a summary of the pirate's history and character, with long reflective set pieces and a rapid, spectacular close.
principal_characters: the corsair; his bride; the captured minstrel; the lord of the isle and his train; the hermit and the convent's inmates
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the outlaw and sea-romance tale, with the minstrel figure and the scene of pursued concealment.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with an interpolated song of the ocean in short lyric measure and a marked use of piling repetition in the passages of terror.
historical_context: Published in 1814, in the last months of the Napoleonic war and in a season of popular appetite for romance of the sea and the pirate, the poem was a commercial event, its first issue of many thousands of copies exhausting itself in a day. It was attacked by the reviewers as a corrupting exhibition of guilty greatness, translated at once into the principal languages of Europe, and dramatized and pilfered in print, which led to an unusual public complaint by its author.
literary_significance: It made the outlaw hero the dominant figure of popular European romance, and its combination of crime, conjugal devotion and spectacular burning scene set the pattern for the century's melodrama and its successors. It is also the best document of the relationship between a famous name, a bookseller's market and a reading public, and its pirated theatrical versions became a case in the argument about the property of the drama.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the text was revised in the collected editions, and the poem's separate 1816 issue with its tale of the lake survives in differing states.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1814 in a large first issue, printed for the author and sold by his regular publisher, with a prefatory 'Advertisement' on the romance's improbability; it appeared in collected volumes the same year and was soon reprinted in translation across Europe.

title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the Third
description: The first canto written after the poet's separation and departure from England, and the point at which the travel poem becomes a soliloquy. Harold reappears at Waterloo and on the Rhine, but the canto's centre is the Lake of Geneva, where the scenery of glacier, lake and mountain draws out a confession of guilt, endurance and self-forgetting. The scheme of the fictional pilgrim is all but abandoned in favour of the poet's own voice, and the water and ice of the Alps are treated as the only language adequate to a mind under public judgment.
plot_or_argument: The pilgrim arrives at the field of Waterloo, where the recent battle supplies the theme of imperial rise and wreck, and moves down the Rhine among the castles and vineyards of the German romantic past. On the Lake of Geneva the travel scheme gives way to meditation on the glacier, the depth and velocity of the lake, and the mountains, and to the poet's own history of a marriage collapsed and a name made notorious. At the valley of Chamounix the canto reaches its argument that the soul has a kindred in the abyss of ice and water, and that solitude is at once loss and liberation; it closes with the pilgrim turning again toward the south. The suppressed stanzas, removed from the first text, made the domestic reference explicit and were restored only long afterward.
narrative_structure: A single canto of progressive meditation, loosely held by the traveler's route, in which the pilgrim recedes and the poet-speaker takes over; it ends in a farewell to the lake and an apostrophe to the mountain scenery.
principal_characters: Childe Harold; the poet-speaker; the presiding spirit of Geneva; the waters of the lake and glacier, addressed as companions
literary_form: Romantic travel poem and lyric meditation in the Spenserian stanza, with the sublime scenery essay and the confession of the divided mind.
meter_and_prosody: Nine-line Spenserian stanzas, iambic pentameter with a closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc; the canto's characteristic movement is a long descriptive period resolved by the twelfth line, with frequent apostrophe and personification.
historical_context: Written in the year of the poet's permanent exile, at the lake where he had stayed with his party in the summer of 1816 and where the glacier journey was made, and published late in that year at a moment of intense public curiosity about his domestic history. Waterloo and the Rhine gave the canto its political frame in the first months of the second restoration, and its treatment of marriage, guilt and the world's judgment was read as autobiography by every reviewer.
literary_significance: It turned the Byronic travel poem into the Romantic meditation on water, mountain and self-forgetting, and became the rival within the poetry of exile of the great lake school's own nature meditations. Its quotations formed a popular vocabulary of solitude, and its history of suppression made it the standard example of the Victorian bowdlerization of a famous text.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the first issue differs from the manuscript in the removal of several stanzas bearing on the poet's marriage, and the erased lines survive in a fair copy and were printed in the collected scholarly editions.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1816 in the volume containing the short pieces written at the lake, sold by the poet's regular house, with a prefatory advertisement; the suppressed stanzas were first printed from the manuscript in the later collected editions.

title: The Prisoner of Chillon
alternative_titles: The Prisoner of Chillon, and Other Poems
description: A dramatic monologue of confinement, founded on the actual imprisonment in the castle of Chillon of a Swiss cleric who resisted the forced adoption of a new faith. The prisoner recounts seven years in a single pillar-girdled dungeon beneath the lake, the deaths of his brothers, and his own passage from prayer to apathy to a freedom that arrives only with his release. It is the period's most influential poem of political and physical confinement, and its blank verse deliberately imitates the colloquial weight of the older drama.
plot_or_argument: Chained to a pillar in a vault where the lake beats above and the steps of his keepers are the only sound, the prisoner watches his brothers die and finds at last that he can no longer grieve; he becomes part of the dungeon, his very chains familiar, and his thoughts turn to the forest and the lake. His gaoler marks the change and fears for his reason, then the chain is loosed, and he goes free into a world that seems his prison still. The argument is that tyranny is measured not in suffering but in the loss of feeling, and that the liberated man carries his confinement as a habit of mind. The closing invocation pardons the keepers and refuses the politics of the crime.
narrative_structure: A single continuous soliloquy in fourteen stanzas of unequal length, chronological within the captivity, framed by a brief prose preface naming the historical prisoner and the castle.
principal_characters: the prisoner of Chillon; his two brothers who die in chains; the gaoler who observes his change; the church and cantonal powers named in the preface
literary_form: Dramatic monologue and poem of confinement in blank verse; the cloistered or dungeon meditation, with the historical preface used to license the fiction.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, five-beat iambic lines with frequent triple endings, weak endings and enjambment, in an intentional reproduction of the manner of the older English drama; the prose preface is set apart from the verse.
historical_context: Written in the summer of 1816 after a visit to the castle on the Lake of Geneva, in the months of the poet's exile and of the restoration settlement that made religious and political imprisonment a live European question, and published in the same season in a volume with the shorter lyrics and meditations of the Swiss journey. Its subject, a Reformed champion confined by a cantonal authority, allowed the poem to be read as a parable of every post-war confinement.
literary_significance: It became the century's touchstone poem of solitary confinement, much imitated in the prison and asylum verse of the following decades, and a central text for the Romantic analysis of the mind's adaptation to oppression. Its borrowed dramatic manner also shaped the development of the modern monologue, and its preface is a document of the Romantic use of history as licence.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem first appeared in a volume of short pieces, and its text was lightly revised in the later collected editions.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1816 in a small quarto volume containing this poem and other pieces, printed for the author and sold by his regular publisher, with a prose preface on the history of the castle and its prisoner.

title: Manfred
description: A closet drama in three acts, styled by its author a dramatic poem and set in the high Alps about a lord of the Simplon who has a past he will not name. Summoning the spirits of earth and water and the lord of the underworld, he learns that he is beyond their reach because his guilt is of his own knowing; the deaths of a beloved spirit and of the woman he loved bring the poem to his own resolute and unassisted end. It is the most exact statement of the school the quarterly critics called Satanic, and its preface defends the poem's unfitness for the stage.
plot_or_argument: Manfred, alone in the tower over the glacier gorge, calls the seven spirits of nature and then the power that rules them, and is told that his secret sin is already forgiven by a being he will not address. He refuses penitence, summons the demon of the place, and is mocked by the witch of the Alps, who loves him and is powerless. News comes of the death of the spirit he has loved, and then of the woman whose loss made him what he is; the last act brings the hermit of St Bernard and a deputation of the country, and Manfred dies refusing the rites they offer, mastering his terror by an act of will. The argument is that a self-conscious guilt can be expiated only by the mind that bore it, and that the imagination of powers greater than the soul may be a disease of knowledge.
narrative_structure: Three acts of scenically arranged soliloquy, invocation and dialogue, each opening with an incantation or chorus; the action is minimal and the poem advances by visions, addresses and the arrival of messengers.
principal_characters: Manfred, lord of the Simplon; the seven spirits of nature; Arimanes and the herald of the underworld; the witch of the Alps; the lost beloved; the hermit of the Great St Bernard; Lionello, a tenant of the valley
literary_form: Closet drama and Romantic mystery in blank verse, with the lyric hymn, the choral invocation and the supernatural machinery of the older drama turned to a psychological end.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines for the dialogue, with irregular lyric measures, refrains and choral songs for the incantations; the versification is deliberately colloquial and weighty, after the manner of the elder English drama.
historical_context: Chiefly written on the tour through the Bernese Alps in September 1816, the year of the poet's separation and exile, with the third act rewritten in early 1817; its treatment of an unpardonable and unnamed offence was read at once as autobiography, and the quarterly press used it as the specimen of a school of poetry it denounced as impious. The preface's claim that the poem was unfit for representation made it an early document of the Romantic closet drama's quarrel with the Regency theatre.
literary_significance: It is the period's central dramatic study of the overreaching, self-condemned mind, and its model of a hero who refuses both forgiveness and despair was inherited by the later dramatic poems of the decade and by the century's treatment of guilt. Its lyric hymns and invocations, set to music later in the century, entered the concert repertoire, and its preface remains a standard text on the Romantic renunciation of the stage.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the text was lightly revised in the collected editions, and the author's own notes on the machinery are printed with it.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1817 in quarto by the poet's regular house, with a preface on the poem's relation to the stage; it was reissued with the other dramatic poems in the collected editions and, in the same year, pirated in the United States.

title: Beppo
description: A light narrative poem in ottava rima, founded on an anecdote the author had heard in Venice, which tells how a long-absent husband returns to find his wife established with a lover and, instead of the expected tragedy, gives them both dinner. Its irony, its digressions on Carnival, the opera, the Pope and English manners, and its refusal of the sensational ending made it a new kind of popular poem. It is the first full exercise of the conversational, laughing manner that the later romance of Spain and England was to carry to its limit.
plot_or_argument: The Genoese captain, pressed into pirate service, has been absent fourteen years, and his young wife has consoled herself with the lord of the house next door; the Carnival supplies the mask and the opera the occasion of their happiness. The captain returns unlooked for at the very moment when a knife has been produced in jealousy, and after a scene of astonishment the three sup together, and the poet reports the neighbours' verdict on the adventure. The argument, carried by constant digression, is that life is more comic than romantic, that the expected catastrophe of the tale of jealousy is a convention of books rather than of Venice, and that the reader's appetite for sensation is part of the subject.
narrative_structure: A single continuous narrative of sixty stanzas, interrupted at every turn by the poet's own digressive address on the theatre, the Carnival, the Pope, and the habits of the English, so that the frame of comment is larger than the tale it suspends.
principal_characters: the Genoese captain; his wife; her lover, the master of the house; the friend who tells the story; the neighbours and Carnival crowd
literary_form: Romantic narrative romance in ottava rima; the conversational verse tale and mock-romance, in deliberate opposition to the serious oriental tale of the same authorship.
meter_and_prosody: Ottava rima, seven iambic pentameter lines rhyming abababcc, with the closing couplet used for point and aside; the manner is easy, colloquial and heavily dependent on enjambment and the abrupt rhyming turn.
historical_context: Written in October 1817 during the Venetian sojourn and issued early in 1818 by a publisher who printed it from a sent manuscript without waiting for the author's final consent, the poem appeared between the serious pilgrimage canto and the great romance of Spain. Its defence of the Carnival, the opera and the domestic arrangements of Italy against northern censoriousness was a deliberate provocation to the quarterly review public, and the preface's apology for its levity became a document of the controversy over a poet's duty to be serious.
literary_significance: It introduced ottava rima and the ironized narrator into English Romantic narrative, and supplied the technical means for the later digressive romance; its handling of the marriage plot as comedy rather than tragedy of jealousy widened the range of the verse tale. It also showed the reading public that the maker of the outlaw hero could write conversationally and laugh at his own reputation.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the printing history is unusual rather than disputed, the first issue being produced by the publisher without the author's final approval.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1818 in a small quarto by the poet's regular house, preceded by a prose advertisement on the truth of the anecdote; it went through several issues that year and was reprinted in the collected poetical volumes.

title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the Fourth
description: The last and most finished canto of the pilgrimage poem, and the one in which the travelling hero disappears altogether, leaving the poet alone with the ruins of northern and central Italy and with Rome. It passes from the Venetian lagoon through Padua, Ferrara, Bologna, Florence and Pisa to the city of the dead and the living papal capital, and ends on the Adriatic shore with an address to the ocean. It is the period's most sustained verse argument about the transience of glory and the survival of the mind among ruins.
plot_or_argument: The canto opens on Venice, the Arsenal and the wasted palaces, and mourns a republic drowned by its own oligarchy and by the foreign yoke; it then runs through the memorials of the literary and princely dead at Padua, Ferrara and the Este court, the tombs and exiles of Florence, and the Pisan sands, before reaching Rome. There the ruins, the pope's city, the buried emperors and poets, the dying gladiator and the petrified Niobe supply the argument that earthly power is a spent coin while the mind and the verse that recorded it endure. The pilgrim is finally detached as a figure of the past, and the close turns to the sea, whose restless permanence offers a reason for endurance that no city can.
narrative_structure: A single topographical progression from lagoon to city to shore, organised as a sequence of meditative set pieces on named places, with the apostrophe and the personified address carrying the argument in place of incident.
principal_characters: the poet-speaker; Childe Harold, who withdraws early; the personified cities of Venice and Rome; the dead of Ferrarese and Florentine history; the ocean of the close
literary_form: Romantic travel poem and topographical meditation in the Spenserian stanza; the ruins poem and the philosophy-of-history ode in narrative measure.
meter_and_prosody: Nine-line Spenserian stanzas, iambic pentameter with the closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc, handled with the greatest regularity and command of the four measures in the series; the final stanzas of the ocean stretch the last line for weight.
historical_context: Written largely during the Venetian and Roman residence of 1817-18 under Austrian restoration rule, in a Italy whose principalities had been rearranged by the congress settlement and whose papal government was the subject of daily liberal complaint; the canto's mourning for a lost Venetian liberty and its treatment of the living pope were read as political statements. It was published separately in 1818, the first canto to appear without the earlier ones, and its reviews were drawn into the quarrel over the poet's character.
literary_significance: It is the summit of the period's ruins meditation and gave English verse its most quoted lyrics on transience, the sea and the endurance of the mind; the canto's treatment of Italy became the template for the century's verse on Italian places. Its withdrawal of the fictional pilgrim also marked a decisive shift from Romantic narrative to Romantic meditation, and its measure was imitated by the long poems of travel that followed.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the canto was revised for the collected editions, and the manuscript and first issue differ in a number of passages bearing on contemporary persons.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1818 as a separate quarto by the poet's regular house, and collected with the three earlier cantos in the issues of the following year; the standard scholarly text records the revisions made for the collected editions.

title: Mazeppa
description: A Cossack tale of the wild ride in couplets, told by an old hetman to a young page: as a passionate courtier of a Polish magnate's household he was punished for an intrigue with the lady of the house by being bound naked to the mane of her own steed and set loose over the Ukraine steppe. The horse's headlong ride, in which the rider's wild hair and his own nails tear him, ends with the fallen pair in the woods of the Dnieper, and the tale passes from punishment to flight to the rise of its hero to the headship of his nation. Its energy, its treatment of shame and endurance, and its landscape of the wild ride made it one of the most reprinted of the tales.
plot_or_argument: The hetman explains why his grey hair and scarred brow are not the marks of years but of a single night's punishment, and describes the noble household, his own youth, and the love that was discovered. The lady's husband sentences him to be fastened upon her own horse, the swiftest and fiercest of her studs, and the animal bears him away across the steppe, over rivers and through forests, while the riders give up the pursuit and the sun burns and the wolves follow. The exhausted horse falls at last in the wilds of the Ukraine, and the Cossacks of the Zaporozhian camp nurse the outcast back to life, so that the punished lover becomes the chief of his people and the ally or enemy of czars. The argument is that suffering can be converted into renown, and that the passions that destroy a man in a drawing room can make a leader in the field.
narrative_structure: A framed narrative, the tale told by the aged hero to his page in three movements, the household exposure, the ride, and the recovery and elevation, with the opening and closing stanzas of the frame returning to the camp.
principal_characters: the aged Cossack hetman; the Polish magnate; the lady of the house; the wild steed of the Ukraine; the Zaporozhian Cossacks who tend the outcast
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the wild-ride and outcast-founding legend, with the framed recitation and the northern or eastern ballad subject.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with a fast running line and anapestic substitution in the ride; the interpolated song of the ride is in short popular measure.
historical_context: Written during the Venetian residence of 1818 and published in the summer of 1819, in the year of the first cantos of the great romance of Spain and of a European vogue for Cossack and Ukrainian material drawn from the history of Charles the Twelfth. Its subject of a punishment inflicted by a jealous husband on a nobleman, and its treatment of a free horse-nation's camp, spoke directly to a public fascinated by the politics of the eastern Europe, and its fame produced prose and stage versions within a decade.
literary_significance: It gave the century its most vivid narrative of pursuit and endurance, and its image of the rider bound to the speeding horse became a stock of painting, music and popular recitation. Along with the earlier tales it fixed the outlaw's elevation from shame to power as a Romantic plot, and its couplets are the most sustained example of the serious use of the heroic measure in the 1819 phase of the verse tale.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the tale is dated in the poet's own memorandum prefixed to the text, and the first issue was made up with a separate lyric ode on the same authorship's Italian city.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1819 in quarto by the poet's regular house, issued with a short ode on an Italian city and dated by an authorial memorandum to the autumn of the preceding year; a prose advertisement cited the historian of the Swedish king as the source of the anecdote.

title: Don Juan
description: The unfinished romance in sixteen cantos that rewrote the libertine legend as a story of a young man who is pursued rather than pursuing, and who is carried by shipwreck, captivity, war and court life through the whole geography of contemporary Europe. Its narrator laughs at every convention it passes, the sentimental, the romantic, the heroic and the fashionable, and its ottava rima gives the digression the same dignity as the incident. It is the largest comic poem in English between the mock-heroic age and the Victorian period.
plot_or_argument: Removed from his school and shipped from Cadiz after an exposure in his mother's house, Juan is cast on a Greek island, loved and lost at sea, rescued by a pirate chief's daughter, sold into a harem in the south, and delivered at last to the camp before a besieged black-sea town, where his bravery wins the favour of an empress. She sends him on a mission to the capital, from which he escapes to the English fleet and reaches an England of country houses, drawing rooms and cant; the last cantos observe the great, their marriages, their duels and their dinners. Throughout, the poet quarrels with his own public, with the review press, with the fashion of sorrow and with the poets who succeeded to the laurel, and the dedication opens the poem with an insult that the publishers feared to print.
narrative_structure: Sixteen cantos in continuous ottava rima, episodically progressive and held together by the narrator's voice; the first canto and its dedicatory preface state the poem's principles, and the later cantos break off in the middle of an address as the author's death ended the work.
principal_characters: Juan, a Spanish youth; the lady of the Seville intrigue; the pirate's daughter of the island; the southern harem lady; the empress of the northern court; the English lord and his fashionable circle; the narrator who appears as a character
literary_form: Romantic verse romance and mock-epic satire in ottava rima; the libertine tale retold as a comedy of convention, with the digressive narrator of the familiar essay inside the romance.
meter_and_prosody: Ottava rima, seven iambic pentameter lines rhyming abababcc, carried at a speed rare in the measure, with the closing couplet used for irony, for sententious aside and for the suspension of the story.
historical_context: Begun at Venice in the late summer of 1818 and continued at Ravenna, Pisa and Genoa until the author's death in 1824, the poem answers the fashionable sentimental novel, the quarterly moral criticism of the previous tales, and the laureate school's providential verse. Its first two cantos appeared anonymously in 1819, the next three in 1821, and cantos six to sixteen were issued by a different house from 1823 to 1824, the main publisher having withdrawn; the notoriety of the author's domestic history made every canto a political event, and the poem was widely pirated and suppressed in lending libraries.
literary_significance: It is the period's supreme achievement in comic narrative verse and the fullest Romantic critique of Romanticism's own postures, and its measure and digressive freedom were taken up by every later English poet attempting ironic romance. Its treatment of the slave trade, of war, of the harem and of the English country house made it a resource for the century's arguments about empire, gender and fashion, and its unfinished state has been a permanent challenge to editors and critics.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the posthumous cantos were printed from manuscripts and fair copies, and the editors of the collected editions record the author's own cancellations, several of which were suppressed in the first issues for legal caution.
bibliographical_notes: First issued in London in 1819, cantos one and two in a handsome quarto printed for the leading publisher of the day and sold anonymously; cantos three to five followed in 1821 from the same house, and the remaining cantos were published from 1823 to 1824 by a second publisher, the last appearing after the author's death. The standard scholarly text is the variorum complete poetical edition with its separate volume of apparatus.

title: Cain
description: A dramatic mystery in two acts which rewrites the first murder as a story of knowledge and disobedience rather than of jealousy. The spirit of the day-star, Lucifer, takes the first ploughman to the spaces beyond the earth and shows him the eternity of the world and the emptiness of the worship demanded of his family; when the accepted offering is refused and the brother slain, Cain is marked and sent out over the eastern land. The poem was read as an attack on providence and became one of the most denounced texts of its year.
plot_or_argument: The family of the first parents, driven from the garden and labouring under a law of offering, are divided in their temper, the elder impatient of a worship whose violence he cannot praise. Lucifer, who refuses adoration and is therefore exiled, teaches him the history of the earth's former ages and the procession of spirits, and shows that the deity who claims his brother's fleece is one among powers, not the maker of all. The offering of the fruit is despised and the favored brother killed at the altar of stone; Cain, questioned by the voice from the cherubim, replies that he is his brother's keeper only in the sense the murderer is, and is marked and condemned to wander, while his wife is promised that the fruit of her womb shall not be cut off. The argument is that obedience to a demanded sacrifice, not the act of murder, is the origin of the world's guilt.
narrative_structure: Two acts of dramatic dialogue with chorus, opened by an address to the morning star and closed by a vision of the coming race; the scene shifts from the tent and altar to the high place of the world and back.
principal_characters: the first ploughman; his sacrificed brother; their mother; Lucifer, the spirit of the day-star; the archangel of the flaming sword; the chosen bride of the wanderer
literary_form: Closet drama and mystery in blank verse; the biblical re-visioning of the school of the older visionary drama, with the chorus and the spectacular ascent of the older religious play.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines for the dialogue, with lyric hymns and choruses in short measures; the manner is deliberately plain and close to the speech of the English version of scripture.
historical_context: Written at Ravenna between January and May 1821, in the season of the Neapolitan and Piedmontese uprisings and their suppression and of the quarrels over the theology of the age, and published in the same December in a single volume with two other dramatic poems. Its treatment of the fall and of the acceptability of sacrifice was taken as a defence of infidelity by the quarterly and religious press, and the volume's own preface, in which the poet affected to be astonished at the offense, deepened the attack.
literary_significance: It is the Romantic period's most influential rewriting of the Cain story and a central document of the poetry of secular questioning, the text by which the charge of a Satanic school was made concrete for a generation of readers. Its elevation of disobedient knowledge over demanded sacrifice was answered by the devout poets of the later century and its machinery, and its two-act design became a model for the modern closet mystery.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume containing it appeared without its author's own preface of advice, and the text was lightly revised in the collected editions.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in December 1821 in a single volume containing two other tragedies, from the regular publisher of the day; the poem had been read in proof before publication and was attacked in the religious and quarterly press within weeks.

title: Marino Faliero
description: A five-act historical tragedy in blank verse on the doge of Venice who, after an insult to his wife is punished by the oligarchy with a merely facial sentence, joins a conspiracy against the ruling council and is himself tried and beheaded. It was written to obey the classical unities of time, place and action, and its preface argues for that restraint as a principle of dramatic truth. The result is a tragedy of private honour set against public justice, the most disciplined of the period's historical dramas.
plot_or_argument: A young patrician writes a satire on the aged doge's elevation, and the council of ten, to which the offender belongs, condemns the writing and not the writer; the insult to the princess his wife drives Faliero to join a plot whose real motive is his own wrong rather than the people's grievance. His fellow conspirators are betrayed by one of their number, the state arrests them in the courtyard, and the doge is tried by the very body he meant to destroy and condemned to die on the palace stairs. The argument is that a private passion cannot be made the engine of a public revolution and that the state's law, which survives all its magistrates, executes even the head it placed. The closing scenes give the doge his composure and the survivor's wife her pardon.
narrative_structure: Five acts observed with a strict unity of place and continuous time, the exposure of the insult early, the plot's betrayal in the fourth act, and the sentence and death in the fifth; the action is carried by dialogue and not by spectacle.
principal_characters: Marino Faliero, doge of Venice; his wife, the princess; the patrician writer of the libel; the leader of the conspiracy; the informer; the councillors of the ten and the advocate of the state
literary_form: Historical tragedy in the classical unities, with the preface as a statement of dramatic theory; the Venetian conspiracy drama of the republican tradition.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, close and speech-like, with an unusual proportion of stichomythia and no songs or supernatural machinery.
historical_context: Composed between April and July 1820 at Ravenna and Venice from the chronicles of the fourteenth-century doge's conspiracy and execution, and published in 1821 in an issue accompanied by a letter to the publisher on the unity of time, place and action. It reached the London stage within months of publication, at a theatre then under pressure of regulation, and its failure there was used by the review press as evidence that the poet's dramas were unreadable on the stage it had condemned.
literary_significance: It is the period's most exact attempt to write a modern tragedy on classical formal terms and a key text in the argument between the closet drama and the regulated Regency stage. Its treatment of a head of state executed by his own institutions was influential in the later historical drama of the century, and its prefaced letter became an anthology piece of Romantic dramatic theory.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the printed text varies from the manuscript in passages of the constitutional debate, and the theatrical versions altered the ending for the stage.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1821 in the volume containing the other Venetian and oriental pieces of the same season, with an epistolary preface on the unities; it was acted in the same year in the metropolis, and in a revised acting text.

title: The Vision of Judgment
description: A satirical dream-vision in sixteen cantos of couplet and stanza, written in answer to the laureate's devotional poem on the death of a late king. The poet dreams the great jury-day at the gate of heaven, where a king's soul is pleaded for by the devil, who is admitted as counsel, and where the assembled saints and worthies, including a Spanish mystic's borrowed vision, decide the case by acclamation. Its target is not the deceased but the machinery of canonization, court poetry and the politics of providence.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer sees the sun put out, the earth wandering dark, and the generation of the dead rising to the judgment; a banner borne by a devil, and a court of heaven crowded with patriarchs, kings and a blackened Spanish friar's procession, precede the trial of a monarch's soul. The accuser's brief is read, the devil's answer is heard and approved, the Virgin intercedes, and the jury of worthies vote the soul to glory by a majority that the dreamer finds unjust. The poem closes with the awakening, a reflection on the value of such visions, and a satire on the poets who sell their measures to the state. The argument is that the machinery by which heaven certifies a king is the same machinery by which the court and the review press certify a reputation.
narrative_structure: A framed dream vision in a continuous sequence of stanzas, the opening on the cosmos out of joint, the trial in the middle, and the waking commentary and personal digression at the end; the borrowed Spanish vision is cited as the source and then mocked.
principal_characters: the dreamer-poet; the soul of the departed king; the devil as counsel for the defence; the recorders of the court of heaven; the Virgin as advocate; the Spanish mystic whose vision is the poem's pretext
literary_form: Augustan verse satire and mock-heroic vision; the dream-vision of judgment turned to political and literary satire, with the Latin and Spanish pretext of the older learned burlesque.
meter_and_prosody: A rolling measure of four-line stanzas in the manner of the older romantic burlesque, with anapestic substitution, triple rhymes and a colloquial velocity; passages of couplet and of mock-sublime blank verse are used for irony.
historical_context: Written in 1821 in direct reply to the laureate's vision of judgment on the death of the late king in the previous year, at a moment when the regulation of the stage, the prosecution of seditious printing and the patronage of court poetry made the connection of piety and politics a live grievance of the liberal press. The poem first appeared over a Castilian pseudonym in the opening number of the short-lived periodical founded by the poet with a London editor, and unauthorized issues naming its author circulated in the same year.
literary_significance: It is the period's boldest satire on the alliance of throne, altar and laureateship, and the work by which the mock-heroic manner of the previous century was revived for Romantic political argument. Its fate, pseudonymous in print and denounced on every hand, became the standard case of prosecution anxieties about blasphemy and libel, and it fixed the poet's reputation as the champion of the irreverent in European politics.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously over a pseudonym borrowed from a Spanish satirist; attribution rests on the periodical's own history and on the author's letters, and is uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1822 in the opening number of a liberal periodical issued in London, over the name of a Spanish satirist, and soon reprinted in unauthorized forms carrying the true author's name; the text was revised for the collected editions of the following year.

title: The Necessity of Atheism
description: The earliest printed work of its author, a short pamphlet of sixteen pages issued at a seaside town in the first months of his undergraduate career and the occasion of his dismissal from the university. It argues that belief in a creator is not a matter of evidence but of habit, that every chain of reasoning must stop at the limits of sensation, and that the hypothesis of a god explains nothing. Its tone is that of the schoolboy metaphysician, aggressive and compressed, but its premises are those the poet was to hold all his life.
plot_or_argument: The pamphlet begins by refusing the burden of proof, since a negative cannot be demonstrated, and then argues that all human knowledge is built on the relation of sensation and idea, so that no evidence of a first cause is accessible. It presses the impossibility of accounting for the existence of matter and the still greater impossibility of an uncaused creator, and closes that a being all-powerful and all-good would be incompatible with the evils of the world. The concluding pages deny that atheism breeds the moral laxity the apologists assume, and insist that inquiry, however unsettling, is the only ground of a reasonable faith. The argument is throughout a train of short propositions with the manner of a college disputation turned against itself.
narrative_structure: A continuous pamphlet argument in numbered propositions, opening with a plea for the freedom of inquiry, passing to the epistemological case, and ending with a challenge to the reader to disprove the conclusion.
literary_form: Polemic and pamphlet prose in the dissenting tradition of the freethinking broadside; the juvenile metaphysical essay with its apparatus of propositions and its appeal to the booksellers' conscience.
meter_and_prosody: Prose; the style is sententious and abrupt, with short declarative sentences, rhetorical questioning and the cadence of the abstract printed for discussion.
historical_context: Printed at Worthing in 1811 and offered through the Oxford booksellers who sold the author's earlier joint volume of verse, the tract was the ground on which he was summoned before his college and, refusing to disown it, was dismissed in the March of that year. Its appearance falls in the season of the statutes against blasphemous and seditious writing, when unitarian and deist pamphlets were prosecuted, and the incident made an undergraduate's metaphysics a public scandal.
literary_significance: It is the founding document of a lifelong radicalism and the reason its author's university career ended in dismissal, an event that shaped the whole later biography and the poetry of the outlaw intellect. Its epistemology, that the mind can reason only from the data of sensation, reappears in the mature philosophical prose, and the pamphlet remains the standard case in the history of academic discipline and of the English freethinking tract.
attribution_notes: Attribution long contested: the title page carried no name, the author refused to own the tract before his college, and an early biographer and a schoolfellow were credited with a share in it. Modern scholarship accepts the main text as the work of a single undergraduate hand, with the schoolfellow's participation unproven.
bibliographical_notes: First printed at Worthing in 1811 for the booksellers of the university town, in a thin octavo of about sixteen pages, without the author's name; reprinted in the collections of the author's prose issued after his death, and in a twentieth-century scholarly edition of the early tracts.

title: Queen Mab
description: A philosophical poem in nine cantos, privately printed in the author's twenty-first year and withheld from the trade during his lifetime, in which the spirit of the elvish queen of dreams carries a lover's soul through the past, present and future of the world. It shows the rise and wreck of religions and dynasties, the corruption of commercial society, and a coming age without priests, kings or gold. Its elaborate notes on necessity, on the vegetable system and on the ancient world are part of the work's design, and its fate as a pirated cheap classic of the movement press made it the most politically famous poem of the century.
plot_or_argument: Under the influence of the poppy-drawn dream and the visitation of the fairy queen, Ianthe's soul is borne above the earth and shown the history of its governments and faiths, the procession of dead monarchs and the tyrants of the present. The middle cantos attack the marriage law, the priests and the merchants, and the moral economy of a society that makes hunger a crime, before the vision passes to a future revolution that restores nature to humankind. A closing canto on the distant stars and the eternity of mind brings the vision to an address to the poet's own land and to the youth who are to inherit the change. The argument is that the world's evils are the work of institutions and not of nature, and that a reasoned hope is a duty.
narrative_structure: Nine cantos of visionary travel, opened and closed by the framework of the dream and the waking, with a sustained apparatus of prose notes that carries much of the philosophical argument independently of the verse.
principal_characters: the fairy queen of dreams; Ianthe, the lover visited by the vision; the ghosts of kings and priests; the spirit of nature; the poet's own address to his country
literary_form: Romantic philosophical vision-poem and didactic romance in the Spenserian stanza, with the annotated programme poem of the radical school.
meter_and_prosody: Spenserian stanzas of nine iambic pentameter lines with the closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc, used for rapid visionary enumeration; the notes are prose, occasionally elevated to rhetorical periodicity.
historical_context: Written largely in the spring of 1813, in the year of the author's flight to Ireland and his connection with the circle of the old dissenting philosophers, and printed in a small private run of some 250 copies that the author distributed at cost. It reached print properly only after his death, when a pirate issued it in a cheap edition alongside a companion tract on diet, an event that brought a prosecution against the publisher and made the poem the touchstone of the republican press through the mid-century.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of the author's radical vision and, through its nineteenth-century cheap reprints, one of the most widely read poems of the labour and freethought movements, exercising an influence on popular politics out of all proportion to its literary standing. Its union of a theory of necessity, a critique of institutional marriage and religion, and a millenarian history gave the later revolutionary odes their shape.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the author disowned the poem in later years in a letter, and the text exists in the private first issue and in the pirated and collected editions of the 1820s and 1830s, with substantial differences.
bibliographical_notes: Privately printed in London in 1813, in a small quarto of about 250 copies, without the authority of a trade publisher and without the author's name; first published for the trade in pirated editions of the early 1820s, and admitted to the author's own collected poetical volumes only in 1839.

title: Alastor; or, The Spirit of Solitude: And Other Poems
description: The first volume of verse issued through the trade by its author, dominated by a long narrative of a poet who dies of the pursuit of an ideal form he once saw in a dream. The title poem states the case for and against imaginative solitude in a single fable, and the accompanying pieces, sonnets, a blank-verse meditation on the sea and the recollections of an unrequited devotion, display a manner learned from the older lake school. Its reviews were severe and the volume sold poorly, and the book marks the point at which a philosophical radical began to write as a poet of mood.
plot_or_argument: A young poet, nurtured by the Genius of the lonely mountains and refusing the company of human love, walks the earth in pursuit of the ideal beauty once shown him in a vision, passing through the caves and valleys of the north and the plains of Asia. He finds at last, by a stream in a desert valley, the form he sought in the likeness of a dead woman who was his mother's love, and dies in the act of clasping the shadow, while his wild companion the eagle and the hind mourn over the stream. The shorter poems add the poet's own creed, the power of the intellect and of beauty, and the consolation of the mountain scenery remembered in absence. The argument is that imagination which refuses the human bond consumes itself, though the poem's own rhetoric admires the refusal.
narrative_structure: A frame of an evening fireside and a winter storm introduces the long narrative in continuous blank verse, with the lyric and sonnet pieces of the volume printed after it and an authorial advertisement in prose.
principal_characters: the solitary poet of the title; the Genius of the mountains; the mother beloved of his infancy; the eagle and the hind of the desert stream; the fire-side hearers of the frame
literary_form: Romantic narrative meditation in blank verse, with the conversation poem and the sonnet sequence of the revived school; the volume is the apprentice statement of a theory of imaginative self-sufficiency.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly blank verse of five-beat iambic lines with rich compound adjectives and long periodic movement; the shorter pieces are Pindaric or Spenserian stanzas and sonnets after the revived manner.
historical_context: Written largely between the autumn of 1815 and the spring of 1816, in the months of the author's first marriage and his withdrawal from his family, and published in 1816 with a prefatory advertisement that complained of the coldness of the metropolis; the review of the volume by the anti-Jacobin quarterlies attacked its egoism and its atheism together. The book's failure pushed the author toward the more public and philosophical verse of the following years.
literary_significance: It gave the century one of its definitive parables of the dangerous self-sufficiency of the imaginative mind, and its title figure was at once read as the poet's own portraiture, making the volume a founding document of the Romantic myth of the solitary genius. Its diction, a deliberate reproduction of the older nature school's compound style, is the clearest record of that school's conquest of the younger generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume's shorter pieces include work of the author's schoolfellow in the accompanying advertisement's account, but the title poem and the principal lyrics are single-handed.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1816 in octavo by the house that issued it with an authorial advertisement in prose; it went through several nineteenth-century collectings and is now read from the standard edition of the poetical works.

title: Mont Blanc
alternative_titles: Mont Blanc: Lines Written Near the Source of the Arve
description: The period's great poem of the high mountain and of the power it exercises over a mind that has abandoned the religious account of the world. Written in a few days beside the glaciers of the Arve, it makes the mountain the emblem of an impersonal power, 'the wilderness of death', and asks what the dreaming mind contributes to the landscape it beholds. Its argument is carried by a series of reiterations and revisions rather than by a progression, and its closing question about the voice of the unseen power is the century's most quoted statement of secular awe.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins at the source of the Arve, where the ravine and the icy summit overhang the poet, and passes to the meditation that the same power which dwells in the mountain speaks also through the human mind, so that the scene is the joint creation of nature and imagination. The middle sections picture the avalanche, the glacier, the dead sea of ice and the small creeping things of the valley, and argue that what seems a wilderness of death is a harmony to the power that perceives it, while to the human sense the same spectacle is annihilation. The close addresses the mountain as the type of an enduring power, and asks what the vale, the heaven and the lake of the poet's own mind have to do with the dream he must be content to have dreamed. The argument is that the sublime is an encounter with a power that the mind can neither deny nor personify.
narrative_structure: A continuous meditation in five unequal movements, from the source of the Arve to the summit and back to the poet's own valley, proceeding by restatement and self-correction rather than narrative.
principal_characters: the poet-speaker beneath the mountain; the personified Power that dwells in the wilderness of snow; the Arve, the glacier and the avalanche as agents; the eternal quiet of the mountain
literary_form: Nature lyric and meditation in blank verse; the sublime scenery poem of the philosophical kind, with an account of the imagination's share in the landscape drawn from the Geneva school of sensation.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, with a heavy use of repetition, assonance and the re-entering phrase, and a famous slackening of the measure in the passages of the avalanche and of the wandering clouds.
historical_context: Composed in a few days of the July of 1816 during the Alpine tour made with a small party on the Lake of Geneva, in the year of the iceless summer that followed the Tambora eruption and of the poet's own separation from his first wife's family circle; it first appeared in print attached to a narrative of the tour published the following year. Its philosophy of the power behind nature was formed in the same months as the essays on necessity and the translation of the classical dialogues.
literary_significance: It is the central English poem of the secular sublime and the period's most exact account of the mind's share in making the landscape it admires, and its argument has been the starting point of most later discussion of Romantic imagination theory. Its treatment of a power without personality or mercy answered directly the lake school's own great meditation on the same region, and gave the century its alternative to a providential reading of the mountain.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was first printed inside a travel narrative written jointly with the poet's companion, and its text varies between that issue and the posthumous collected volumes.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1817 as an appendix poem to a narrative of an Alpine tour, in octavo, and not collected in a volume of verse during the author's lifetime; it was established in the canon by the posthumous poetical collections and by the twentieth-century standard edition of the manuscripts.

title: The Revolt of Islam
alternative_titles: Laon and Cythna; or, The Revolt of Islam
description: The largest of the author's long poems, a revolutionary romance in Spenserian stanzas set in a southern caliphate whose people rise against their priests and kings. Two lovers, a man and a woman of the ruling house, preach reason and liberty from a car of the mind, survive the stakes and the flood, and are destroyed at the moment of the city's deliverance by the armed intervention of a holy confederacy. It appeared first under one title with an argument for free love and was withdrawn and reissued, with the offences expurgated, as the present poem.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with a dream on a moonlit sea, a vessel, a victory and the death of the tyrant, and passes to the tale of the two lovers, who were taught by a hermit the creed of reason and who, on emerging from a cave of learning, preach a new faith of love and liberty to the multitude. The caliph's priests burn the woman in the market-place and the man is bound to the same pile, but the two are saved by a vision of the world's future; the city rises, the throne of the despot is burned and a free council meets. The lovers at last die of wounds received in the counter-attack of the confederate kings, and the poet awakes on the sea with the vision unfinished. The argument is that the revolution of the mind is stronger than the stake, but that its triumph is always bought with the death of its teachers.
narrative_structure: A dream frame on the ocean, an argument in prose prefaced to the original issue, and twenty-nine cantos of continuous narrative, with inserted hymns, chants of the earth and spirit and a long philosophical speech on the past and future of the world.
principal_characters: the two lovers of the title, a prince and a maid of the caliph's blood; the hermit teacher of the cave; the priests and the caliph of the city; the Demogorgon of the cavern of human thought; the wingless thing of the vision
literary_form: Romantic verse romance and political vision poem in the Spenserian stanza; the revolutionary tale of the school of the earlier long poems, with the hymn and the choral ode inserted.
meter_and_prosody: Spenserian stanzas of nine eleven-syllable lines, ababbcbcc, sustained over a very great length with an increasing freedom of the caesura; the inserted chants pass to shorter lyric measures.
historical_context: Written chiefly between the spring and the autumn of 1817, in the years of the continental settlement, of the suspension of the habeas corpus and of the persecutions following the northern march of the reformers, and of the poet's own removal to the seaside and then to London. It was issued late in 1817 over its first title, withdrawn by the publishers within a few weeks on account of its treatment of religion and of sibling love, and reissued in January 1818 with nearly two hundred lines cancelled or altered. Its sales were negligible, and the poet's response was to turn to the shorter and denser forms of the following years.
literary_significance: It is the most ambitious attempt of the period to fuse a revolutionary argument with the machinery of romance, and its history of withdrawal and expurgation is the best document of the pressure of the blasphemy and libel laws on long verse. Its treatment of the failure of a revolution from within, of the martyrdom of teachers and of the hope that survives it, shaped the later political odes and the drama of the unbinding.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the two states of the text, that of 1817 and that of 1818, are both authorial, and the cancelled passages were recovered from the proof sheets and manuscript by modern editors.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1817 in octavo, with a prose preface on the French revolution and the creed of the poem, under the earlier title; reissued in January 1818 as the present poem with the offending passages cancelled, the sale of either state being very small. The standard text follows the manuscript and the first-state proofs.

title: The Cenci
description: A five-act historical tragedy in blank verse, founded on the chronicle of a Roman count who murdered his children's father with the help of his stepmother and was for that crime executed by the papal court.
