Its preface uses the story to argue for a drama of human passion rather than of allegory, and the tragedy sets a father's violation against a daughter's duty and a state's justice. It is the period's most sustained attempt to write revenge tragedy without its machinery, and the most terrible treatment of tyranny within the family in Romantic drama.
plot_or_argument: A father returning from banishment discovers his estates seized and his wife and daughters ruined by his own expense, and resolves on a vengeance which he conceals from his son and reveals only to God's ministers as a duty. The son is murdered on a mountain pass by the hired ruffians and thrown into a lake, and the father, fearing discovery, violates his daughter, whose long denial and final appeal to the law fail before the corruption of the courts. Her stepmother then persuades the household servants to the murder, the body is carried to the chamber and stabbed in the night, and the trace of the crime is found in the rings that were melted from the fingers. All are tried at the papal court, tortured and condemned, and the daughter, her mother and her brother are executed, while the last act shows the survivors' fate and the poet's own comment on the justice that avenged the first crime.
narrative_structure: Five acts of continuous tragedy in the classical manner, the violation deferred and reported rather than shown, the murder in the fourth act and the trial and executions in the fifth, with a choral comment carried by the surviving sister.
principal_characters: the Roman count, the father and tyrant of the house; his first wife and her daughter; the stepmother who plans the murder; the elder son and the younger daughter who dies with them; the hired ruffians of the pass; the papal judge and the officer of the law
literary_form: Revenge tragedy and domestic tragedy in blank verse, without supernatural machinery; the historical crime tragedy of the Italian chronicle tradition turned to a study of violated duty and of state justice.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, deliberately plainspoken and close to dialogue, with short stichomythic exchanges in the trial scenes and only a few lyric passages.
historical_context: Written at Rome and Naples in 1819, in the year of the poet's permanent settlement in Italy and of the executions and imprisonments that followed the failures of the Italian risings, and published in the same year with a preface on the difference between the ideal and the practical drama. Its matter came from a sixteenth-century Italian chronicle, and its treatment of papal justice and of paternal authority was a direct provocation to the Catholic and Tory reviews. It was read privately to a circle of friends in London in 1821, an event sometimes recorded as its first representation.
literary_significance: It is the strongest of the period's closet tragedies and a central text in the argument about whether the Romantic drama could be acted at all, its preface supplying the period's sharpest defence of character over allegory. Its treatment of sexual tyranny within the patriarchal house and of the failure of legal remedy anticipated a permanent theme of later literature, and its daughter remains the century's most terrible figure of wronged endurance.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the text was lightly revised in the posthumous collections, and the acting manuscript differs from the printed first edition in passages of the trial.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1819 in octavo, with a preface of some length on the theory of tragedy and on the chronicle from which the story was taken; privately read before an audience of friends in the capital in 1821, and not professionally staged until long after the author's death.

title: Prometheus Unbound
alternative_titles: Prometheus Unbound: A Lyric Drama in Four Acts
description: The author's masterpiece, a four-act lyrical drama which rewrites the old myth of the stolen fire as a history of the mind's deliverance from fear. The titan, tormented on the Caucasus and sustained by hatred of the tyrant heaven, is taught by the spirit of the earth and by an oceanic vision of the future, and the act of renouncing his curse releases the power that ends the reign of the king of the gods. Its preface states a theory of poetry as the record of an imagination in action, and its fourth act is a pure choral cosmology.
plot_or_argument: Prometheus, chained and fed by the ocean nymphs, refuses to reveal the secret that would save or ruin heaven's king, and his furies of hate are soothed by a vision of a coming love. Demogorgon, born of the hour and sitting in the cave of eternity, declares the law of change, and the titan, learning that his victim's suffering was not his triumph, withdraws his curses and is thereby free. The tyrant is swept from his throne by the hours, Hercules releases the eagle-wasted prisoner at the sound of the earth's rejoicing choirs, and Asia and Prometheus are crowned in the caves of the atoms, from which the last act sends the regeneration of the world abroad.
narrative_structure: Four acts, the first two of dialogue and prophecy, the third of the catastrophe and the crown of the heroes, the fourth an epilogue of choral cosmology; the argument advances by address, hymn and vision rather than by action.
principal_characters: Prometheus, the titan of the stolen fire; Asia, his love and the type of the awakened mind; Jupiter, the tyrant of heaven; Demogorgon, the power born of the hour; the spirit of the earth, the ocean waves and the hours; Panthea and Ione and the satyrs
literary_form: Closet drama and lyrical drama in the classical mask form, with the choral hymn, the epilogue and the philosophical prefatory essay; a re-visioning of the older Promethean tragedy.
meter_and_prosody: A vast range of measures, regular blank verse for the titan's speeches, and lyric stanzaic forms, cantos of short lines, triple rhymes and refrains for the spirits and choirs; the fourth act is almost entirely song.
historical_context: Begun at Naples in the winter of 1818-19 in a house by the bay, and completed in 1819 during the poet's stays at Rome and in the Tuscan baths, in the months of his exile among the ruins of the papal states and of the European reaction after the risings in Italy and Spain were suppressed. It was published in 1820 with the short poems of that season and received almost no notice; its own preface, an answer to a critic's charge that poetry must inculcate moral feeling, became part of the work's argument.
literary_significance: It is the period's great poem of liberation from the theology of fear and its most ambitious fusion of dramatic, lyric and philosophical form; its fourth act supplied the template for the poetry of elemental process. Its preface and its practice together define the theory of imagination as a way of knowing, and its politics of non-violent renunciation has been a permanent resource for later radical readings.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; an earlier and shorter draft of the first act, begun before the final design, survives and is printed as a fragment in the standard edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in a small octavo volume containing the shorter odes and lyrics of the same season, from the house that had issued the author's earlier verse; the preface to the volume, on the defence of poetry, is the earliest printed form of the author's critical theory.

title: Ode to the West Wind
description: A five-part ode addressed to the autumn wind, which at once destroys the year's leaves and carries the seed to its springing, and which the poet asks to make the instrument of his own regenerative power. Written in the woods beside a river in a stormy October, it converts the description of air, water and earth into an argument about the poet's function. Its closing prayer, that the dead thought may quicken a new birth, is one of the most quoted passages of English lyric, and the terza rima sonnet structure of its parts is a technical monument.
plot_or_argument: The ode addresses the wind first as the destroyer of the leaves and the carrier of the dead seeds to their winter graves, then as the spirit in the air, in the waves of the sea which it rouses and in the forest whose loose hairs it shakes. The poet then asks to be made one with the wind, a leaf, a wave and a cloud, and to be scattered like the ashes and sparks from an unextinguished hearth among mankind. The final part turns the prayer to speech itself, an exhortation that the blasts of the dead thought may wake the sleeping earth, and the poem ends with the promise of the returning spring. The argument is that the poet's power is not his own but the wind's, and that the same force which buries the year also germinates it.
narrative_structure: Five sections of fourteen lines each, the first three describing the wind's action on earth, air and water, the fourth and fifth passing to the poet's own prayer; the movement is from cosmology to vocation.
principal_characters: the wind addressed as spirit; the dead leaves and the winged seeds; the waves of the Atlantic and the sea-mosses; the poet who asks to be the wind's lyre
literary_form: Romantic ode in the revived lyric form, combining the elemental hymn of the school of the earlier odes with the personal prayer of the meditation; an ode of vocation.
meter_and_prosody: Fourteen-line sections built of four tercets and a closing couplet in the third-rhyme measure of the older Italian sequence, iambic pentameter, a structure that binds the argument tightly and forces the close into a couplet.
historical_context: Composed in the Arno woods in the October of 1820, in the year of the poet's settlement near Pisa, of his failing health and of the Neapolitan rising and its crushing by the Austrian arms; the season's storm over the river is reported as the occasion. It appeared in the 1820 volume of the shorter poems and drew little attention there, its fame belonging to the later anthologies.
literary_significance: It is the period's most influential elemental hymn and the standard example of how a Romantic ode can fuse description, argument and prayer in a single strict form. Its closing figure of the dead thought scattered to quicken a new birth gave later revolutionary and educational poetry its most portable image of the intellectual's function.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the ode was printed in the author's lifetime and has been reedited from the manuscript with the interleaved corrections noted.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume containing the lyric drama of the titan and the shorter poems of the Italian season; a contemporary prose note on the wind's character was prefixed by the author to the separate draft.

title: To a Skylark
description: The period's most quoted hymn to an invisible bird, addressed to a skylark rising out of the English meadow into the unfelt air and singing as it ascends. The poem reasons from the bird's joy to the condition of the human mind, which can only imagine pleasure it cannot feel and which forebodes pain even in its mirth. Its structure of twenty-one stanzas with a recurring short closing line gives it the character of an incantation, and it was written, by the poet's own account, from a walk on the shore near the Tuscan city where he then lived.
plot_or_argument: The bird, hailed as a spirit rather than a bird, hides in the blue deep of the sky and is known only by the sound that falls like hail, like moonlight, like a glow-worm in the grass. The poem then runs through a series of comparisons, a poet new to his thoughts, a noble damsel in a palace of hushed sorrow, a glow-worm, a rose hidden by its own leaves, rain waking the flowers, and every sweet and joyful sight, before granting that no simile reaches the bird's happiness. The human condition is then set against it, we look before and after and mourn before our mirth is gone, and the poem ends with the prayer that if the bird's spirit were known, the poet's words would not fall dead upon the world. The argument is that the unembodied song measures the distance between nature's joy and human self-consciousness.
narrative_structure: Twenty-one stanzas of continuous address, moving from the ascent to the catalogue of similes, to the reflection on human sorrow and to the closing prayer; there is no story but a single sustained act of attention.
principal_characters: the skylark, addressed as a star of heaven and as a spirit of joy; the poet who would be taught the measure of its thoughts
literary_form: Romantic ode and elemental hymn; the invisible-voice lyric of the school of the greater odes, with the simile catalogue of the devotional hymn.
meter_and_prosody: Stanzas of four iambic pentameter lines followed by a single trimmed tetrameter line, rhyming ababb with the short fifth line repeated as a refrain; the abbreviations of the measure, all but two lines being of fewer syllables, give the stanza its upward momentum.
historical_context: Written in the summer of 1820, in the season the poet spent on the coast of Tuscany after the birth of a son and in the months of the Neapolitan and Piedmontese risings and their suppression, and published in the London volume of that year's shorter poems. Its companion volume of the same season contained the titan drama and the wind ode, and its treatment of inspiration as something granted rather than achieved answered the era's account of the poet's faculty.
literary_significance: It is the best-known of the period's lyrics and became a schoolroom and anthological test of pure rapture in verse, much imitated in the short measures of the later nineteenth century. Its analysis of human consciousness as a creature that looks before and after gave the century one of its most portable definitions of melancholy, and the stanza's structure has been much discussed as a model of the lyric line's upward figure.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; an early prose note on the circumstances of composition was written out by the poet, and the text varies only in small readings between the first issue and the posthumous collections.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume containing the lyric drama of the titan, from the usual publisher of the author's verse, over the hyphenated form of the title; the accompanying preface note on the circumstances of composition has been printed from the manuscript.

title: Epipsychidion
description: A long lyric poem of ideal love, written for a young Italian woman confined by her father in a convent and addressed to her as the visible type of a beauty the poet had sought all his life. It passes from the portrait of the lady to an autobiography of the poet's own successive ideals, to a proposal of a life together on a boat in the Archipelago, and ends in a protest that the poem has mistaken its subject. Its frankness about plural desire and its theory of the mingled soul made it notorious at once and long uneditable.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the portrait of Emily, the winter prisoner of the convent, whose coming has awakened the poet's long-seated passion, and proceeds to an account of an ideal shape of beauty pursued in dream and missed in every mortal form. The middle sections argue that love divides itself into a community of kindred minds, and the poet proposes that the three of them, himself, his wife and the lady, should live together on a small vessel in the southern islands. The close turns against the poem itself, calling it an error and a trespass, and ends with an address to the poet's own verse and to the friends who are to judge it. The argument is that the soul seeks its own type in another and that the union of spirits is not violated by plurality.
narrative_structure: A continuous lyric argument of some four hundred and thirty lines, divided by shifts of address, the portrait, the autobiography of ideals, the proposal of the island life and the penitential close.
principal_characters: the imprisoned lady of the poem's occasion; the poet-speaker; the wife addressed as the second and gentler spirit; the father and the convent that keep the lady
literary_form: Romantic lyric meditation and poem of idealized love, with the autobiographical retrospect of the greater odes and the marriage argument of the prose of the same season.
meter_and_prosody: Predominantly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with frequent triple rhymes, alexandrines and irregular lyric runs; the movement is hurried and the rhymes often strain for the sense.
historical_context: Written at Pisa in the spring of 1821, in the months following the poet's friendship with the liberal circle of the Tuscan city and the visit of the young lady confined by her father, and published in London in 1822 in a separate issue without the author's name. Its account of a three-fold union and its treatment of conventual restraint were at once read as a scandal of private life, and the poet's own friends counselled suppression of the poem; it was reprinted among the posthumous volumes in the following decade.
literary_significance: It is the period's most candid analysis of idealizing love and of the plurality of desire, and a central exhibit in the argument about the poet's relations, domestic arrangements and the ethics of the mind. Its phrase for the mingled soul became a permanent possession of later love poetry, and its history of private printing and friends' remonstrance is a document of the Romantic handling of autobiographical matter.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the first issue was anonymous, and the poem's dedication and accompanying advertisement, which named the occasion, were cancelled before publication.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1822 in a small quarto, anonymous but for the reference to an earlier volume, printed at the instance of a friend of the author; the cancelled dedication and the proofs of the advertisement survive and are printed in the standard edition.

title: Adonais
alternative_titles: Adonais: An Elegy on the Death of a Younger Poet
description: The greatest English elegy of the period, written in a few weeks of the summer of 1821 on the death in Rome of a young poet whom the author had known for four years. It mourns the dead man as Adonis, denounces the reviewers who killed him, and passes in the closing stanzas to a vision in which the mourned soul becomes one with the eternal Beauty behind the world of change. Its fifty-five Spenserian stanzas make it both a personal lament and a statement of a creed of immortality through verse.
plot_or_argument: The poem wakes the year's dead beauty and declares that no spring shall bring back the youth who is lost, and then turns on the fierce city and the cold world that let him perish, and on the review-journal whose tooth had wounded him. The middle stanzas raise a funeral procession of the poets of the age and of the mother's grief, and the mourner reproaches himself for having lived on while the friend was cut off. The close passes beyond consolation to a metaphysic, the dead man is one with the Power from which the light of the world proceeds, and the poet, still held by the dust of life, asks that the fire within him may consume the body's haze so that he may rise where the dreamer's spirit rests. The argument is that early death in a poet is at once an accusation against society and the soul's release into permanent beauty.
narrative_structure: Fifty-five continuous stanzas, opening with the year's lament, passing to invective against the critics and the city, to the procession of mourners and the mother, and to the final self-address and vision of the eternal.
principal_characters: the dead young poet, mourned as Adonis; the poet-speaker who calls himself the saddest of the survivors; the mother of the dead; the fierce city of his death and the reviewers as the hounds that hunted him
literary_form: Elegy and Romantic monody in the Spenserian stanza, with the invective passage of the satirical tradition and the consolation ode of the philosophical lyric.
meter_and_prosody: Spenserian stanzas of nine iambic pentameter lines with the closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc, sustained with a freedom of caesura and a richness of vowel-patterning unmatched in the author's other work.
historical_context: Written at Pisa and at the baths of Tuscany between July and September 1821, on the news of a friend's death in Rome in the February of that year after a journey made in the hope of a milder climate, and printed the same year in a small Italian issue at a ducal press whose type the author had ordered for the purpose. It was attacked for its personal invective in the metropolitan reviews, and its companion prose account of the death, prefixed in a second issue the following year, made the quarrel about the influence of criticism on a sick man a permanent biographical crux.
literary_significance: It gave the elegy its most complete Romantic form and made the early death of the poet a public charge against the review world, an argument that long outlived the quarrel it began. Its closing vision of the soul's unity with the Power behind appearance became a standard of the poetry of consolation, and its measure renewed the Spenserian stanza for the serious monody of the later century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem exists in a first Italian issue and in a second issue with the prefaced prose account, and the posthumous collections reprint the text with small revisions.
bibliographical_notes: First printed at Pisa in 1821 in a small quarto issued in a limited number, from the types of a ducal press, and reissued in a second state the same year with a prose preface on the circumstances of the death; collected among the posthumous poetical volumes published by the author's widow in the following years.

title: Hellas
description: A short lyrical drama written in a few weeks to celebrate the Greek rising against the Ottoman power, and built on the poet's own statement in its preface that its scenery and machinery are drawn from the hills and gulf of the modern Morea. A phantom of the ancient glory of Hellas appears to a worshipper by the sea at Lepanto and shows the regeneration of the race, while the chorus of captive women doubts and the despairing old men answer with the prophecy of a new age. It is the most purely political of the author's dramas and the shortest of his serious verse plays.
plot_or_argument: A devotee of the ancient muse keeps the vigil of the year at Sunium and by the Gulf of Lepanto, mourning that Greece has no voice left, and the phantom of her buried glory rises upon the waters to promise a coming day of deliverance. The chorus of captive women and the despairing chiefs of the race dispute the promise, and the vision passes to the triumph of a regenerated people, the tyrant's power broken and the altars of the free rebuilt. The close retracts the certainty, the poet's own voice acknowledges the doubt of the human heart, and the drama ends with the invocation of the immortal spirit of the scene. The argument is that a nation's ancient memory is the warrant of its political resurrection.
narrative_structure: A dramatic scene of some four hundred lines with choral entry and exit, opened by the devotee's soliloquy, the vision and its questioning in the middle and the retracting close; the movement is entirely lyric and prophetic.
principal_characters: the devotee of the ancient glory; the phantom of Hellas; the chorus of captive women; the despairing chief of the race; the tyrant of the East as the power denounced
literary_form: Closet drama and lyrical drama in the classical masked form, with the chorus of the older Attic tragedy; a political ode cast as a scene.
meter_and_prosody: A variety of lyric measures, free iambic and trochaic lines for the dialogue and short responsive strophes for the chorus, with the anapestic movement of the prophetic passages.
historical_context: Composed at Pisa between October and December 1821, in the months of the outbreak of the Greek revolution, the rise of the eastern question in European politics and the execution of the patriarch, and published in London in 1822 with a prose preface on the poet's design and his own account of the poem's failure to sell. The dedication to the friends who had fought and died in the cause made it a public act of subscription to a foreign war of liberation.
literary_significance: It became the lyrical testament of philhellenism and one of the most recited and quoted political lyrics of the following century, its stanzas used in the cause of Greek and of Italian freedom. Its preface is also a document of the author's late theory of poetry and of his disillusionment with the immediate effect of verse, and its treatment of national memory as a political force shaped the later poetry of liberation movements.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published in the author's lifetime and its text is stable, with minor revisions in the posthumous collections.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1822 in a small octavo volume containing the poem, a prose preface and a translation issued with it, from the house that had published the earlier volumes; the sale was reported by the author's friends as almost nil.

title: The Masque of Anarchy
description: A political poem of ninety stanzas written within days of the cavalry charge on a peaceful reform meeting in a northern city, and withheld from print for more than a decade. Memory, Murder and Fraud ride in a masque with their following of Plagues, Creeds and Laws, and at their head Power, seated on a throne of skulls, announces that whatever is, is right. The poem then turns to an address to the people of England, urging a resistance of folded arms, and it is the first great statement of non-violent mass protest in modern letters.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer sees a pageant marching through the mist of a northern city, a ghost with a mask of gold crying that God and the king and the people are one with its own interest, and behind it Murder with a bald and shining forehead, Fraud holding a blood-besmeared book, and a procession of Plagues, Hypocrisy and Superstition with their laws and creeds. The mask is broken by the appearance of a figure of Liberty who is trampled down, and the poem's second half passes to an exhortation to the thousands who are starving, to rise with their arms folded and let the sabres fall on nothing but the will. The argument is that a people that refuses to strike, and makes the state's violence visible by its own stillness, is the power that cannot be conquered.
narrative_structure: Two clearly marked parts, the allegorical pageant seen in a dream of the northern city and the direct political exhortation addressed to the crowd; the whole is in a continuous four-line stanza of ballad measure.
principal_characters: the dreamer-witness of the pageant; the masked Power at the head of the procession; Murder, Fraud and Hypocrisy as the shapes of the state; Liberty, the trampled woman of the crowd; the assembled people of England
literary_form: Political and revolutionary verse; the allegorical pageant poem and public address, in the ballad measure of the periodical and handbill tradition.
meter_and_prosody: Four-line ballad quatrains of alternating four- and three-beat anapestic lines, rhyming abab, a measure borrowed from the popular and the school of the earlier political song; the repetition of the refrain gives it its force.
historical_context: Written at Leghorn in the September of 1819, within a fortnight of the charge of the yeomanry on the reformers' meeting in the northern city and of the prosecutions and suspensions of public meeting that followed, and offered to a liberal editor who judged it unprintable. It was withheld for more than a decade and published only in 1832, the year of the first reform bill's passage, by the same editor who had declined it, with a prefatory account of its suppression; its delayed circulation among friends influenced the radical poetry of the later century.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of the literature of non-violent resistance and its image of the folded arms was taken up by the labour, chartist and later pacifist movements. Its treatment of a state whose allegorical mask is transparent, and its theory that the governed outnumber the governors in will, remain the most influential Romantic account of popular protest.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the manuscript was copied and read in the author's circle, and a version altered for the publisher's fears survives, the full text being established from the holograph.
bibliographical_notes: Not printed in the author's lifetime; first published in London in 1832 in a liberal periodical, sixteen years after composition, in an issue prepared by an editor who had earlier declined it; the holograph and the expurgated working copy are the basis of the modern text.

title: A Defence of Poetry
description: The period's most influential essay of poetic theory, written in a few weeks as a reply to a friend's prose argument that poetry must inculcate moral truth. It defines poetry as the expression of the imagination, morality as the calculation of the relations of action to effect, and argues that a man who is good must love the beautiful, so that the poet who only creates is the unacknowledged legislator of the world. Its aphoristic manner and its argument for the utility of the useless have made it the centre of the Romantic theory of imagination.
plot_or_argument: The essay opens by accepting that poetry is a branch of the art whose end is pleasure, and then distinguishes reasoning, which tabulates the relations of what is known, from imagination, which represents action as it is affected by the qualities of the mind that contemplates it. It argues that poetry is connected with the principles of our nature by the same ties as language and that the reasoning and the imaginative faculties are as the measure and the harmony of composition. It passes to a history of the civilizing power of poetry, from the ballad and the drama to the great works of the age it lives in, and defends the modern poets against the charge of indifference to moral instruction. Its close asserts that the influence of the poet is all-sufficient, that poetry is the record of the best and happiest moments of the happiest and best minds, and that the world's moral regeneration is the work of imagination.
narrative_structure: A continuous occasional essay in twenty numbered sections, opening with the concession to the opponent's definition, proceeding by distinction, example and historical survey, and closing with the aphorisms on the legislator and on the happiness of the imaginative mind.
literary_form: Critical treatise and occasional essay of the Romantic theory of imagination; a polemical defence written in the manner of the reply pamphlet and enriched by aphoristic prose rhythm.
meter_and_prosody: Prose; a highly rhythmic periodic style, built on balanced clause, reiteration and the sententious closing member, much quoted as prose aphorism.
historical_context: Written at Bagni di Lucca and at Pisa between February and March 1821 in reply to a prose essay, published in a review by a friend, on the demand that poetry should inculcate moral truth, and at a moment when the poet was defending his own longest and most philosophical drama against the charge of irrelevance. It was not printed in the author's lifetime; it first appeared posthumously in a collection of his prose edited by his widow, and its fame belongs to the reprints of the later century.
literary_significance: It is the most compact statement of the Romantic doctrine of imagination and, with its companion essay on the same occasion, the standard text of the defence of poetry's utility against a utilitarian age. Its definition of reason and imagination, and its claim for the poet as an unacknowledged legislator, have governed most later discussion of the social function of literature.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the essay was unfinished, the closing section fragmentary, and the printed text rests on a copy made by a friend of the author in the last year of his life.
bibliographical_notes: Not printed in the author's lifetime; first published in 1840 in a collected volume of the author's prose edited by his widow, in which the essay appears from a transcript, its unfinished conclusion being printed with a mark of omission. The standard scholarly text is the edition of the prose works.

title: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
alternative_titles: On First Looking to Chapman's Homer
description: The most famous sonnet of its author's first season and the document of his poetic awakening: written the morning after an evening spent reading an Elizabethan translation of Homer, and printed a few days later in the weekly journal of the circle that had just discovered him. It declares that the poet had travelled in imagination through the whole library of recognized poetry without finding its Homeric breadth, and that Chapman's version gave him the pure common air of the epics. Its two closing similes, the astronomer and the Spanish observer of the Pacific, made it the standard figure of the moment of literary discovery.
plot_or_argument: The opening quartet reports a borrowed pilgrimage through the regions of art, the western islands of Homer, the bright leagues of Elizabethan romance and the courts and roads of the older poets, all visited in fancy and none of them penetrated. The first tercet names the instant of arrival, the sense of a new heaven and a fine gown of the old eagle, and the closing couplet turns to the two figures of astonishment, the astronomer watching a new planet swim into his ken, and the eagle-eyed stargazer, and the Spanish chief on the peak of Darien looking at the Pacific with a still stare while all his men gaze at one another and look solemn. The argument is that real reading is a discovery of a country, and that the great translation can give a modern reader more of the original's strength than a scholar's fidelity.
narrative_structure: A single fourteen-line argument in the revived Italian form, the two quatrains setting the general proposition of the prior wanderings, the first tercet the crisis of the new sight, and the close running to the twin similes of discovery.
principal_characters: the poet as imaginary traveller; the astronomer descrying a new planet; the conqueror on the Darien peak and his men
literary_form: Romantic sonnet of the revived school; the occasional lyric of literary experience, in the manner of the Leigh-Hunt circle's own sonnets on the arts.
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter in the revived Italian form, the octave closed on two rhymes and the sestet turning through three; the manner is Latinate and plain in the diction of the Elizabethan reading, and the closing sentences are long and cumulative.
historical_context: Composed in October 1816, the fortnight after the poet was introduced to the editor of the Examiner by a friend of the same circle and read an Elizabethan Homer with a schoolfellow in the evening, and printed in that journal on the first day of the following month. Its appearance belongs to the moment when the Hunt circle was making a new poetry of sensation against the review establishment, and the sonnet was at once taken as that circle's programme in miniature.
literary_significance: It became the period's definitive statement that the reading of the classics is a discovery rather than a duty, and its final image of the astronomer and the conqueror is still the common property of the language for the moment of recognition. It also established the author's reputation among his contemporaries before any volume of his appeared, and fixed the relation of the revived English sonnet to the argument about translation and imaginative strength.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the sonnet is dated by the accounts of the writer's friends, and it entered the printed text from the journal in which it first appeared.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in a London weekly journal of politics and the fine arts on 1 November 1816, over the author's name, and reprinted in the first collected volume of poems issued the following March; the manuscript was given by the writer to the editor's circle and survives.

title: Endymion: A Poetic Romance
description: The author's first long poem, a four-book romance of the shepherd who loves the moon and must learn that the love of an immortal and of a mortal are one thing. Its opening sentence, that a thing of beauty is a joy for ever, states the poem's creed of endurance, and the fable of pursuit, despair and discovery is laid out in a succession of epodes, songs, cavils and visions. The book was written in haste and in the country, in the hope of making a living by verse, and its reception in the Scottish and metropolitan journals the same year was one of the mortal injuries of the poet's short life.
plot_or_argument: Endymion, who has won the prize of a contest by the mountain and is loved for it, burns for the sight of the moon and abandons the company of shepherds to follow her shadow over hill, dale and sea. He descends in the second book to an under-water palace, where he is told of a rival's constancy and of his own trial, and in the third is led through a desert and shown the procession of Fancy's children before being warned by a voice that his quest is hopeless. The fourth book sets him in the power of Glory and of the tempter of the earth, from which the love of a woman, who has been given him as a shadow of the immortal, delivers him, and at the last the moon herself accepts him. The argument is that the love of beauty passes through earthly love and that endurance and sympathy are the education of the soul.
narrative_structure: Four books of continuous romance, each opened by an epode or address and diversified by songs, a dream-vision, an under-water scene and a contest in the desert, with a long lyrical epilogue.
principal_characters: Endymion, the shepherd in love with the moon; Cynthia, the moon goddess; the woman who is her shadow; the rival shepherd of the palace; Arethusa and the ocean powers; Fancy's children in the procession
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the elastic Spenserian romances of the older school and the episodic tale poem, with the interpolated song and the allegorical vision.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter of a very flowing and often enfeebled kind, with songs in popular measures and an epode of longer lines; the line's movement is deliberately luxuriant and unargumentative.
historical_context: Written mainly between the spring of 1817 and the January of 1818, at the house of a friend in the country and at the seaside, in the season of the poet's decision to give up the hospital apothecary's profession and live by his pen; it was published in the same year by the firm which had taken him on from the first publisher. Its attack in a Scottish journal and in the metropolitan critical reviews, which treated its luxurious diction as the fault of a school of London cockneys, was the beginning of the public war that the later lyrics and the hyperion poems were written to answer.
literary_significance: It is the richest and most ungoverned of the period's romances in verse, and its creed of the enduringness of beauty became one of the most quoted moral positions of later aestheticism. Its failure in the reviews fixed the biography of the persecuted young poet in the popular imagination, while its diction, its songs and its under-water and desert visions mark the point from which the greater lyrics of 1819 were written.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the drafts and fair copies, several in the hand of a friend, survive, and the poem was revised only slightly for the collections.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1818 in a small octavo, printed for the Fleet Street house which had taken the poet on from his first publisher and dated 1818 on the title page; it went through a second issue the same year and was reprinted in the standard poetical editions from the holograph fragments.

title: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
alternative_titles: Isabella, or the Pot of Basil
description: A short romance in ottava rima taken from a novellieri's tale of the fourteenth century, in which a merchant's sister, married by a trick to a young man of her own choosing, is robbed of her lover by her brothers, who murder him while he sleeps in the woods. The lady finds the body, carries the skull and bones away in a pot of basil, and waters it with her tears until the basil withers and her brothers take it from her. It is the most concentrated of the author's narrative poems and a study of jealous wealth against devoted grief.
plot_or_argument: Isabella, the daughter of a wealthy family of Messina, loves a young clerk of her brothers' house, and by an artifice obtains her marriage to him; the brothers, ashamed of the match and anxious for their fortune, take their brother on a journey and kill him in a forest. The girl, told in a dream where her lover lies, goes to the spot, digs up the body, and carries the skull and bones away in a pot of basil, which she tends and waters, never leaving it, so that the plant grows strangely and the neighbours marvel. Her brothers at last steal the pot from her, and she pines and dies praying that her tomb may hold what they have taken; the pot was never afterwards found. The argument is that a mercantile family's honour can murder love, and that the devotion of grief is a thing which money cannot seize.
narrative_structure: A continuous narrative in some sixty ottava-rima stanzas, the exposition of the family and the love, the murder reported, the dream and the discovery of the grave, and the long middle of the basil's tending, closing on the lady's death and the lost pot.
principal_characters: Isabella, the merchant's daughter; her lover, the clerk of the house; her three brothers of the merchant's honour; the old nurse of the household; the people and priests of Messina
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the Italian novella in English ottava rima, with the gothic and the ballad's treatment of devoted female grief.
meter_and_prosody: Ottava rima, seven-line iambic pentameter stanzas rhyming abababcc, used here with great fluency and a frequent closing couplet of sentiment; the song of the pot is set apart in shorter lyric measure.
historical_context: Composed at the house of a friend's family in the north of London in the February of 1819, in the weeks after the death of the poet's younger brother and during the same season which produced the Belle Dame ballad and the beginning of the titan poem, and published in the 1820 volume. Its choice of an old Italian tale and its scorn for a mercantile brothers' world belong to the same argument about the poetry of sensation as the longer romance of the moon.
literary_significance: It gave the English ottava rima one of its most finished narrative poems and made the pot of basil a permanent image of a grief that tends its own loss; the tale was repeatedly reprinted in the annuals and retold on the stage of the later century. Its handling of a woman's devotion against familial avarice became a touchstone for the discussion of the author's narrative sympathy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is dated by the letters of its composition and exists in a fair copy in another hand made for the printer.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume of the poet's later lyric and narrative work, from the house which had issued the romance of the moon; the poem had been circulated among friends in manuscript before the volume's appearance.

title: Hyperion: A Fragment
description: The author's attempt at a Miltonic epic on the fall of the elder gods, abandoned in the autumn of 1819 and published as a fragment of two books in the volume of that year's poems. The deposed Saturn mourns in the caverns of the old sea, the Titaness urges him to rise, and the ocean-god argues that the elder powers have yielded by a law of gradation to a younger and fairer rule. The second book brings the messenger of the new reign and the assembly of the Titans, and the poem breaks off before the battle and the fall.
plot_or_argument: Saturn, dethroned and hidden in the deep caverns by the mouth of the ocean, laments his lost empire, and the earth-goddess who has kept his company reproaches him for his unmanly grief. The elders debate their condition, and Oceanus answers that no throne is kept for ever, that the elder gods have fallen by gradation from the Titans to the Olympian rule, and that the new order is more beautiful; the voice is answered by the Titan of the east, who refuses the argument. The second book opens on the mourning of the fallen race and brings the rainbow-messenger from the seat of the new god, whose look of settled splendence overthrows the counsel of resistance; the gods deliberate whether to rise, and the fragment ends.
narrative_structure: Two books of continuous epic narrative in blank verse, the first a council and argument in the caverns, the second the arrival of the messenger and the debate; a sketch for a third book and a projected theogony survive in the drafts.
principal_characters: Saturn, the deposed elder god; the earth-goddess his mate and reprover; Oceanus, the arguer of gradation; the eastern Titan of the last line; the rainbow-messenger of the new reign
literary_form: Heroic epic of the Miltonic school, projected as a theogony and left a fragment; the Titanomachy matter of the classical epic in English blank verse.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, loaded with compound epithets, Latinate inversion and a sustained end-stopped dignity designed to imitate the older epic's stateliness; it is the author's only considerable effort in pure epic measure.
historical_context: Begun in the summer of 1818, in the months of the poet's northern tour and of his brother's fatal illness, and worked at through the winter, the poem's argument of the inevitable succession of powers was written in the season of the Italian and Spanish revolutions and their suppression; abandoned late in 1819, its books were published in 1820 in the volume of the later poems with an explicit mark of incompleteness. The poet's own letters on the causes of its abandonment, which turn on the failure of its diction and the impossibility of its Miltonic mask, are among the most searched documents of Romantic composition.
literary_significance: It is the period's most impressive attempt at a non-religious epic and the standard case in the argument about whether the epic could be written after Milton, a question the fragment's own incompleteness answers. Its account of the gradation by which orders of the mind succeed one another became a permanent text for the philosophy of cultural progress, and its diction marks the point where the poet's rich sensuous style begins to be disciplined.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the two published books and the surviving drafts, with the alternative dream-version of the same argument, are all in the poet's hand and are printed together in the standard edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 as the closing piece of the octavo volume of the poet's later work, printed as two books only and marked a fragment; the drafts, with the letters on the poem's abandonment, are the basis of the modern scholarly text.

title: The Eve of St. Agnes
alternative_titles: The Eve of St. Agnes: A Legendary Poem for the Year 1819
description: The author's richest legendary poem, a romance of the eve of a virgin saint whose ritual, in the old belief, let a maiden see the shape of the husband she was to marry. It tells how a youth, banned from the house of his lady's hostile kin, is hidden by an old beadswoman in her room, enters the lady's chamber at the hour of the rite, and is persuaded by the superstition's own power to flee with him. The poem's colour, its treatment of the consecrated sleep and its music of the stanza have made it the most quoted of the narratives.
plot_or_argument: On a night of bitter cold, with the owl and the hare abroad, a youthful lover waits at the door of the hall where a baron's company is feasting, and is admitted by an old woman servant to the shelter of her chamber; his lady's family are foes to his. Madeline, who has kept the vigil and believes that she shall see her promised lord at the rite's hour, is left alone in her rose-casemented room, and Porphyro steals in while she sleeps in the middle of the ceremony's dream. He wakes her with the sound of the charmed company, and after the scene of the feast of the senses the two escape into the storm, leaving the old beadswoman dead at the foot of the altar and the house in confusion. The argument is that the consecrated dream becomes the warrant of an outlawed love, and that the ritual's power is realised in the flesh.
narrative_structure: A continuous legendary romance of forty Spenserian stanzas, the external scene of the hall, the secret chamber, the vigil and ritual in the middle, the escape and the moral close in the last stanzas.
principal_characters: Porphyro, the lover outlawed by the lady's kin; Madeline of the rose window and the vigil; the old beadswoman Angela; the baron and the riotous company of the hall
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the legendary and superstition tale of the school of the older romance, with the ritual scene and the gothic household.
meter_and_prosody: The Spenserian stanza of nine iambic pentameter lines with the closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc, handled with an unprecedented richness of vowel and colour, the rhyme sustained and the last line used for a slow close.
historical_context: Begun at the house of a friend's family in the north of London in the winter of 1819, in the season when the poet was writing the odes and the dream-version of the titan poem, and finished at the seaside in the spring of 1820, appearing in the volume of that July. Its subject, a Catholic superstition of maidens treated with complete sympathy, belonged to the same interest in consecuted ritual which the period's romance and its controversial religion shared, and its archaic diction was a deliberate answer to the reviews which had pronounced the earlier romance the work of a school.
literary_significance: It is the period's supreme example of colour and sense carried by the Spenserian measure, and its stanzas on the casement, the feast and the storm became a stock of the later poetry of romantic intensity. Its treatment of a ritual dream fulfilled in an elopement also made it the central text of the discussion of the poet's relation to superstition and to the consecrated life.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem's early draft survives, and its title and the accompanying legend were explained in a prose note of the poet's own written for the volume.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume of the poet's later work, as the opening piece, with a prose note on the superstition of the eve rite; it was reprinted in the yearly collections of the poet's work from the 1830s onward.

title: Lamia
alternative_titles: Lamia. Isabella. The Eve of St. Agnes. Ode to a Nightingale. Ode on a Grecian Urn. To Autumn, and Other Poems
description: A two-part narrative poem of a serpent-woman who, having been given a human form by the magic of her lover's devotion, is destroyed at a banquet by the cold eye of a philosopher who will not let an illusion stand. It is the author's most polished couplet poem and the subtlest of his statements of the quarrel between the imaginative and the analytic life. Its first part tells the love of Lamia and a young knight of Corinth, its second the banquet and the exposure, and the moral is left unresolved.
plot_or_argument: A serpent of golden grain, who is in truth a woman and who has been seen by a youth of Corinth in the shape of a serpent, is granted her human form by the power of the love she wakes in him, and she builds a palace of cloud and shadow for their dwelling. The pair pass into Corinth as bride and lord of a house, and the lover's friends and the whole city are drawn to the splendour of the feast, while the philosopher Apollonius, asked to the banquet by the lovers, fixes his eye upon the bride and discovers the phantom nature of the palace. At his word the illusions fall away, the bride is seen as the serpent of the field, and the lover dies of the loss; the philosopher goes on his way rebuked. The argument is that the loveliness which the imagination creates may be the only truth by which a human life can be sustained, and that the analytic knowledge which exposes it is not innocent.
narrative_structure: Two parts, the first of some hundred and forty couplets on the metamorphosis and the building of the palace, the second of the banquet and the exposure, with the second part carrying the poem's reflection on the philosopher's office.
principal_characters: Lamia, the serpent-woman of the field; the young knight of Corinth her lover; Apollonius the philosopher; the guests and friends of the banquet; the mother of Lamia named in the exordium
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the fable of the enchantment and the exposure, in the couplet manner of the older romance translation, with the philosophical argument carried by the second part.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of iambic pentameter, handled with extraordinary fluency and a sustained use of the closed line, with short interpolated lyric passages and the famous lines of the exordium in a looser movement.
historical_context: Written in the late summer and autumn of 1819 at Wentworth Place, Hampstead, where the poet lodged with a friend, in the season which produced the great lyrics and the two titan poems, and published in the volume of July 1820 which was his last in his lifetime. Its attack on the analytic coldness of the philosopher was read at once as a squib on the metaphysics of the day, and its treatment of an illusion which knowledge destroys gave it a permanent place in the argument about the value of the imagination.
literary_significance: It is the most complete of the period's couplet romances and the source of the enduring formula for the sacrifice of the world's loveliness to a philosophy of cold analysis. Its two-part design, the enchantment and its exposure, became a model for later poems of the destructive intellect, and its couplets are the standard instance of the poet's mastery of a measure he was accused of not possessing.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was kept for the volume of July 1820 rather than given to the periodical press, and the manuscript and the printer's copy are the basis of the modern text.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume which took its name from this poem, printed for the Fleet Street house and issued in July of that year; the volume contained the narrative poems, the lyrics and the titan fragment, and it is from its title page that the poet's last season is usually described.

title: Ode to a Nightingale
description: The greatest of the author's odes of 1819 and one of the two or three most perfect lyrics in the language, written in the spring at the house of a friend's family in the north of London, after the singing of a nightingale in the garden. It passes from the wish for the draught of vintage that might let the speaker fade away with the bird, through a refusal of the drug of forgetfulness and an argument with the thought of death, to the vision of the bird's immortal song heard by emperor and clown in the old world and in the sea of the biblical past. Its close, waking from the fancy with the question whether the bird was a phantom or a living thing, is the period's most exact statement of divided belief.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens in a numbness of heart as though of hemlock and of Lethe, and the speaker, hearing the full-throated ease of the bird in the dark woodland, asks for a draught that he may dissolve away from the world where palsy shakes a few pale silent nerves and where youth fades and the spectre of illness sits. He will use no chariot of the poet but the viewless wings of Poesy, and in the dark he is with the bird, knowing the flowers and the season by scent and by the fancy of the mother-ward green, and admires the ease of a death in such an hour. But the bird's immortal strain, heard in the old days and on the windows of the hostile camp of the biblical story, is not for the weary hearer, and at the word forlorn the fancy cannot cheat so well as she is famed, so the speaker wakes to his own solitary song and asks whether it was wake or dream. The argument is that the imaginative transport is at once real and insufficient, and that beauty which does not die only measures the pain of what dies.
narrative_structure: Eight stanzas of ten lines, the movement from the numbness of the opening, through the invocation to the bird and the dark transport, to the immortal strain and the awakening; the argument advances by a succession of acts of attention rather than by incident.
principal_characters: the nightingale of the wood, addressed as a bird and as a voice; the speaker who would fade away; the fancy which cannot cheat so well as she is famed
literary_form: Romantic ode of the school of the great odes of 1819, combining the elemental hymn, the meditation on death and the transport of the imagination in a single strict stanza.
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter in ten-line stanzas rhyming abab, the sestet varied with a shortened fourth line of the second half, the structure giving the stanza both its weight and its check; the music of the vowel and the repetition are the poem's argument.
historical_context: Composed in the spring of 1819 at the house in Hampstead grounds where the poet was living with a friend, in the year after the death of his younger brother of consumption and in the season of his own first symptoms and of his love for the woman of the neighbouring house; the nightingale's song in the garden is the reported occasion. It appeared in the volume of July 1820, the last of the poet's lifetime, and its treatment of the thought of death as a release and of the beauty of the immortal bird gave the century its model of the serious lyric.
literary_significance: It established the Romantic ode at its highest and remains the standard example of a lyric whose form enacts its argument, the transport and its collapse being carried by the stanza's own structure. Its account of the bird's song as immortal, heard by the emperors and the clowns of the old world, became one of the most quoted passages of the period, and its division at the close is the classic statement of the Romantic quarrel with the sufficiency of imagination.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem survives in the drafts of the season and in the transcript made for the volume, and the textual questions concern only small readings.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume of the poet's later poems, issued in July by the Fleet Street house; the drafts of the spring of 1819, with the letters of the season on the conditions of composition, are the basis of the modern scholarly text.

title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
description: The companion ode of the same season to that of the nightingale, and the period's most searched poem on the relation of art to life. Addressed to a marble frieze of the old Greek world, the bride of silence, it asks what tale the shapes pursue, and answers itself that the figures, being fixed in art, shall love for ever and shall never be parted, while the lover for ever pines and for ever burns. Its closing sentences, on beauty and truth, have made it a centre of the argument about the poet's creed.
plot_or_argument: The ode begins with the address to the foster-child of silence and slow time, and asks what legend of the old men and maidens, of Thessalian or Arcadian passion, the pictured tale pursues; the shapes cannot be told, and the speaker answers that the far-heard melodies are for the other sense, and that the boughs which never shed their leaves and the for ever singing love are happier than the winning of the heart. The middle stanzas pass to the Sacrificer going to his altar, the green little town which for ever is silent and hollows its streets, and to the beauty which draws the eye and the mind, till the last stanza names the urn Attic and the marble breeding friend of the human race, whose message to a generation like this, being beauty and being truth, is the whole of what it needs to know. The argument is that art's stillness is a truer condition than life's passing, and that the lesson of beauty is the only knowledge given to the troubled age.
narrative_structure: Five stanzas of ten lines, the opening questions, the answer on the unattained love and the for ever burning fever, the vision of the sacrifice and the emptied town, and the close on the urn's message to the aging generation.
principal_characters: the urn, addressed as bride, foster-child of silence and Attic shape; the lover and the beloved of the frieze; the priest and the Sacrificer of the heifer; the little town for ever silent
literary_form: Romantic ode and ekphrasis of the school of the great odes of 1819; the poem on a piece of ancient art turned to a meditation on the permanence of the work against the passing of the beholder.
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter in ten-line stanzas, the first four lines alternating and the sestet varied, with the shortened line of the second half of the stanza used for check; the diction is compressed and the questions of the opening give the poem its movement.
historical_context: Written in the spring of 1819 at Wentworth Place, Hampstead, where the poet lodged with a friend, in the same season as the ode of the nightingale and the two titan poems, and published in the volume of July 1820. Its subject was drawn from the old Greek marbles then a possession of the metropolis and from the engravings of the classical vase, and its identification of beauty with truth was at once, and has remained, the most quoted and most disputed statement of the poet's creed.
literary_significance: It is the period's supreme poem on the silent speech of the visual arts and the source of the most quoted and most analysed closing lines in English Romantic writing. Its treatment of art as a condition at once enviable and inhuman set the terms of much later discussion of aesthetic doctrine, and its stanza has been the standard model of the English ode in the century after.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem exists in the drafts of the season and in the transcript of the volume, and its disputed sense has never been a question of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume of the poet's later poems issued in July by the Fleet Street house, printed from a transcript; the drafts of 1819 and the letters of the season are the basis of the scholarly text.

title: To Autumn
description: The last of the great short poems and the closing piece of the volume of 1820, a lyric of three eleven-line stanzas which presents the season not as the prelude to death but as a condition of ripeness and of its own music. It personifies autumn as the close friend of the maturing sun, as the harvester resting by the half-reaped furrow and as the gatherer of the last gleanings, and answers the questions of the spring with the sounds of the day of departure. Its stillness, its freedom from argument and its handling of the transience of the year have made it the most admired short poem of the period.
plot_or_argument: The first stanza presents autumn as the neighbour of the sun that ripens the fruit and fills the gourd and the hazel shells with kernel, and as the season that makes the swags bulge and the cyder press drop the last oozings. The second finds the season itself at rest, sitting on a half-reaped furrow, winnowing on the floor, and sleeping by the harvest cider-house while the last gleanings cross the brook, and the third asks where are the songs of spring, and answers that the listener has his own music in the wailful choir of the small gnats, the bleating lambs, the crickets and the swallow. The argument is that the season of decay has its own completeness and that the music of departure is not an absence but an instrument.
narrative_structure: Three stanzas of eleven lines, the first of ripening, the second of the season at rest in the harvest field, the third of the sounds of the evening of the year; there is no development but a change of aspect.
principal_characters: autumn personified as the close friend of the maturing sun, as the reaper, the winnower and the gleaner, and as the hearer of the season's own choir
literary_form: Romantic ode and nature lyric of the school of the great odes; the seasonal meditation and the hymn of the year's departure, in the most concentrated form the period reached.
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter in three stanzas of eleven lines, the rhyme abab and the remainder varied, with the closing line of each stanza used as a caesura of rest; the poem is almost free of metaphor of the violent kind and depends on the verb and on the article of detail.
historical_context: Composed on a Sunday in the September of 1819, on a walk in the fields near the town where the poet was staying with a friend, in the season of his last effort at the titan poem and of the beginning of his illness, and printed in the volume of July 1820 as one of the closing pieces. Its date, after the abandonment of the larger work, made it the symbol in later biography of a short career's harvest, and its freedom from the argument of the greater odes was widely imitated in the seasonal lyric of the later century.
literary_significance: It is the most complete and most quoted of the period's short poems, and the standing example of a lyric that presents a process without a moral and a death without lamentation. Its handling of the personified season gave the later nature lyric one of its permanent registers, and the sequence of the three odes and this poem forms the schoolroom definition of the Romantic lyric at its limit.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is in the transcript of the volume and is dated by the poet's own letters of the season.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1820 in the octavo volume of the poet's later poems issued in July by the Fleet Street house, near the end of the contents; the manuscript, in the hand of the transcript, is the basis of the scholarly text.

title: The Fall of Hyperion: A Dream
alternative_titles: Hyperion. The Dream of the Poet
description: The dream-version of the titan poem, in which the poet himself becomes the speaker and the fall of the elder gods is witnessed as the vision of an aspirant to the office of poetry. Written in the late summer and autumn of 1819 and left unfinished, it recasts the earlier epic as a monody of the poet's function, in which the mortal pain of the world is the qualification for the immortal work. It was never printed in the author's lifetime and first appeared from the manuscript in the middle of the following century.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer, awake in an old thought and heavy as the leaves of autumn, finds himself in a temple of the dead gods where the stones breathe and the columnar spaces seem alive, and climbs the steps to the shrine where Saturn and the Titan race lie as in the earlier poem. There he meets the guide Moneta, the shadow of the faintest worn lady of the tribe, who shows him the priest's office and forbids him to touch the altar, declaring that no one may enter the lists of the immortal but those who suffer for the human race, the high souls who are the physicians of its pain. As the dreamer tries to speak the tale of the fallen gods the scene passes to the last vision of the poem, and the fragment ends with the question of the dreamer's own waking office. The argument is that the poetry of the immortal is bought only by the mortal pain of the world's misery.
narrative_structure: A single continuous dream vision with a dream frame, opening on the speaker's fevered condition, passing to the temple and the address of Moneta, and breaking off in the middle of the poet's attempt to tell the titan tale.
principal_characters: the dreamer-poet; Moneta, the guide and priestess of the shrine, the shadow of the old seer of the tribe; Saturn and the fallen Titan race of the earlier poem
literary_form: Dream vision and Romantic monody of the poet's function, recasting the Miltonic titan fragment as a vision of the priestly office of the imagination.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, with a far more colloquial and self-questioning movement than that of the earlier epic draft and a heavier use of the enjambed line and of the parenthetical address.
historical_context: Written in the late summer and autumn of 1819 at Wentworth Place, Hampstead, where the poet lodged with a friend, in the season of the great odes and after the abandonment of the first titan draft, and never completed nor printed in the author's lifetime. Its definition of the poet as the physician of the world's pain belongs to the same months as the letters on negative capability and on the vale of the world's making, and it became the central text of the argument about the two versions of the titan poem.
literary_significance: It is the period's most searching account of the poet's vocation as a suffering office, and its claim that only those who live for others may enter the lists of the immortal became one of the most quoted propositions of later poetics. Its recovery in the middle of the nineteenth century and its relation to the earlier draft have made it the standard instance of the Romantic poem existing in two authorially distinct versions.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem survives in a manuscript and in transcripts made by the author's friends, and its relation to the earlier draft was long disputed by editors before the manuscripts were fully printed.
bibliographical_notes: Never printed in the author's lifetime; first published posthumously in the mid-nineteenth century from the manuscript, appearing in the third series of a bibliographical society's collections printed in 1856-57 over the title of another version of the titan poem, and admitted to the collected poetical text only in the later scholarly editions.
